summary: Seven element headers in one night, and the build gates found two numbers on live cards that need a ruling plus three kinds of scanning damage in the sealed books -- all now blocked from reaching a reader.
detail:
Seven whole element headers were designed overnight instead of the usual one, and the interesting part is not the count -- it is that building them found two numbers on live cards that need Luneth's ruling, and three separate kinds of scanning damage in the sealed books that are now blocked from ever reaching a reader.

SCOPE. Seven deep header rounds in one night -- germanium (27 claims), lithium (27), vitamin B3 (25), vitamin B9 (24), vitamin B1 (23), manganese (19), vitamin D (18) -- chosen as the next seven by claim count with no deep round yet, verified against the corpus rather than taken from the handoff. 49 panels. Lithium had no research dossier and was read cold.

METHOD. Unchanged from the four-element round and it held: quotations sliced from the sealed verbatim by marker at build time so a drifted source kills the build; numbers parsed by regex from the verbatim, never transcribed; lists split from their own verbatims so the printed order is the book's; symbol and slug expansions cross-checked against each claim's OWN sealed essentials/conditions field rather than a hand-typed key; an id gate proving every cited id is sealed and linked to that element. New this round: every finding is computed and asserted, so 'four of five land on 50 mg', 'the only row below the RDA' and '13 of 16 entries in both books' are gates rather than copy.

THE TWO RULINGS THAT CHANGE LIVE CARDS. Vitamin D is the sharpest number problem this project has found. Across the 24 rows of his 1995 base-line table the build can parse, vitamin D is the ONLY row where his own figure is LOWER than the government RDA -- 275 IU against 400. His 2011 book separately caps total intake at 400 IU/day for cerebrovascular disease. His 2014 book gives 1,000-2,000 IU and the card takes the upper: 2,000 IU, which is 7.3x his 1995 figure and 5x his own 2011 ceiling. Every figure is his and favour-newest is applied correctly; what is unusual is that the books disagree about DIRECTION rather than size, on a vitamin whose toxicity entry in his own table is calcification of the arteries. Separately, folate's 400 mcg target is numerically identical to the RDA printed in column one of his 1995 row -- the column he reprints in order to argue against it -- while his own true supplement need in that same row is 1,000 mcg. Folate is the one essential whose card and the RDA coincide. Neither ruling was made here; both are asserted in the generators so the build dies if either figure moves.

THE CORPUS FIND. Three classes of scanning damage in sealed verbatims, measured across all 2,255 claims rather than estimated. Nineteen line-break hyphen artifacts, derived by evidence: a mid-word hyphen counts only when the joined form appears elsewhere in the corpus unhyphenated, with genuine hyphenations named in an allowlist. Eight occurrences across seven claims of the digit 1 read as a lowercase L. Twenty occurrences across eighteen claims of a space before a thousands comma. All three now fail the build. The shared gate is wired into qs() itself so no generator can bypass it, and it fired three times in production during this run -- each time the panel was rebuilt to quote a different clause or to render the parsed value instead of the damaged sentence. The seal was not touched; corpus_seal is USER-ONLY and repairing the source is his call.

WHAT THE INSTRUMENTS GOT WRONG. The build gates caught my own code more often than the data: an Oxford comma that left the final list item as 'and cancer' and under-counted germanium's four-book agreement; a three-line table wrap that invented a phantom nineteenth niacin sign; a splitter that turned dietary instructions into mineral chips. The DOM probe reported 'TEXT COLLISIONS: none' on six real defects that screenshots caught, including a label sitting on a curve and a value label clipped off the edge of a figure. And a scroll probe that read window.scrollY immediately after a wheel reported 0 and looked exactly like the standalone scroll-lock -- it was the instrument, not the page.

STATE. Board 88/88 with no new reds, 23 external / 23 consistency / 40 structural / 2 meta. Corpus sealed and untouched -- no mining, no re-seal, no claim edited. Nothing ported live and nothing picked. No tracked file changed outside chronicle/; every generator, fragment and page is in gitignored temporary/. Index at temporary/_overnight-2026-08-04.html.

summary: Luneth: a contradiction between two of Wallach's books is not a finding to present -- favour-newest settles it silently. Vitamin D 2,000 IU is correct; folate is the one case where the older book wins and the 2014 400 mcg is likely a misprint.
detail:
Luneth corrected the framing of the round I had just closed: a disagreement between two of Wallach's books is not an interesting finding to show a reader, it is something the favour-newest rule already settles. I had built two lead panels out of exactly that, so the handoff was rewritten before the next session could inherit it.

RULING 1 -- CONTRADICTIONS ARE NOT FINDINGS. His words: 'You need to stop bringing book contradictions front facing as if they're some fun thing worth presenting, this is ABSURD. We ALWAYS favor the newer book numbers because Wallach learns and changes his stance over time, so any contradiction DEFAULTS to the newest one.' The favour-newest rule was already in the project; what I got wrong was treating its INPUT as editorial material. A revision is evidence that the author was paying attention, not a defect to dramatise. Resolve silently. The only time a contradiction is worth raising is when the NEWEST number is itself suspect, and then it is a defect report rather than a panel.

VITAMIN D IS SETTLED. 50 mcg / 2,000 IU is correct, corroborated outside the books by his own Ultimate Classic formula using exactly that amount. The whole lead panel of the vitamin D round -- 'the one number he moved the other way' -- rests on a premise that does not survive the ruling, along with its why-line and lede. It must be replaced, not patched.

RULING 2 -- FOLATE IS THE ONE EXCEPTION, AND IT RUNS THE OTHER WAY. Epigenetics (2014) prints 'Folic acid 400 mcg'; Let's Play Doctor (1995) gives a true supplement need of 1,000 mcg. His ruling is that the newer figure must be a misprint, because he has multiple supplements that go over 1,000 mcg, so 400 cannot be his position. His hypothesis is that the page reads 1,400 and the scan garbled it.

WHAT I COULD AND COULD NOT ESTABLISH TONIGHT. He asked me to confirm against the book's actual PDF or image. There is none in this repository -- eden/corpus/books/ holds seven .txt files and nothing else, and no page images exist for Epigenetics -- so the confirmation cannot be made from what is here and needs the real book. What I did establish: the row sits at char_offset 1414086, between the screenshot markers for Page 816 and Page 818, so it is on Screenshot 674 / Page 816 of 936. And one piece of counter-evidence worth carrying to the page rather than assuming past: TWO rows in that same table are a bare '400 mcg' -- Folic acid and Vitamin B12 (methylcobalamin) -- while all fourteen other vitamin rows are ranges. A single OCR digit-drop producing the same wrong value twice in one column is less likely than one of them being genuine, so the page has to settle it either way.

NO SEAL. The three OCR damage classes found earlier tonight are gated out of the demo generators but are untouched in the corpus itself, so the conditional permission to seal does not apply. Nothing was sealed. corpus_seal remains USER-ONLY and unexercised this session.

summary: Folate's live target was wrong and is now right: 400 mcg -> 1,000 mcg. Luneth read the real Epigenetics page; the book itself misprints, so the 2014 claim was deleted rather than guessed at, and the app falls through to his 1995 number.
detail:
The card said folate 400 mcg. That is exactly the government RDA -- the number Wallach spends his books arguing is far too low -- so seeing it posted as HIS recommendation was the tell. The open question was whether the scanner had garbled the page or the book really printed it. Luneth read the actual page. The book really prints 400. So this is not a scanning error to repair, it is a misprint in the book, and there is no correct number visible on that page to put in its place. Rather than invent one, the claim was deleted -- and because the app always prefers the newest book, deleting the newest claim makes it fall through to the 1995 book, where Wallach spells out 1,000 mcg in his own table. No special case anywhere in the code.

The part worth remembering is what the deletion nearly took with it. Every claim can carry one search entry, and this claim's entry was the app's only answer to 'How much folic acid should I take?' -- the most obvious question anyone would type about folate. Deleting the claim without noticing would have silently removed that answer, and the board would have stayed green, because no gate knows a question is missing. It also turned out that answer had been describing a DIFFERENT claim's numbers all along -- it was attached to the wrong claim. It now hangs off the right one.

TECHNICAL RECORD. Deleted WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000123 (epigenetics, char_offset 1414086, verbatim 'Folic acid 400 mcg\nCholine 10 - 100 mg\nInositol 10 - 100 mg\n', dose 400 mcg daily, for_condition 'daily multiple vitamin and mineral supplement program'). Measured BEFORE the write that it and WAL-CLM-LETS-000052 were the only two vitamin-b9 dose claims across all seven books, and read targets_derive's picker (max_year, then priority, then id) to confirm the fall-through rather than assume it. Result on disk: essentials-targets-data.json vitamin-b9 low=1000.0 mcg, source_claim_id=WAL-CLM-LETS-000052, other_claims=None. Sibling rows of the same 2014 table are untouched -- EPIGEN-000122 (biotin), -000124 (choline), -000125 (inositol) -- and choline/inositol keep their 10-100 mg targets.

Purging a claim is TWO deletions (mining-mechanics section 6): the search-enrichment sidecar must go with it or search_index_derive refuses to derive. That sidecar was the corpus's only protocol-facet vitamin-b9 entry, and its answer_short recited LETS-000052's three columns (400 RDA / 1,000 true-need / 15-20 mg) while its own claim carried a single 400 mcg figure -- proof it was mis-attached. Re-homed onto LETS-000052. Enrichment is strictly one entry per claim (2247 dicts, zero lists), so the re-home displaced that claim's inositol question; safe, because WAL-CLM-LETS-000053 is a real inositol dose claim carrying the same 90 mg, and inositol retains 2 protocol questions plus 8 others. also_about set to [] deliberately: the Q&A is wholly about folate, so keeping it on inositol's page would have surfaced noise.

Luneth then rejected the wording as inside baseball and was right. It was in two places, and the SEALED claim_text was the worse one -- its back half explained how to read the table's column order, which is a note to ourselves, not an answer. Rewritten via mine_batch (the sanctioned draft editor; claim_text is an agent-owned field) and safe_write (answer_short). Every figure still traces to the claim's own verbatim, and 'two and a half times' is computed from 1000/400, not transcribed.

Recorded as ratified-divergences entry 74, class book-misprint-deletion, carrying the deleted verbatim and offset so the deletion is recoverable and cannot be mistaken later for a mining gap. corpus_seal was USER-AUTHORISED this session (it is user-only every time): sealed at knowledge_version=459, 2254 claims, corpus_verify PASS. build_embeds regenerated all 15 artifacts; build.mjs 0; invariants 88/88, 0 failed, no new reds -- 23 external / 23 consistency / 40 structural / 2 meta, and green means nothing drifted, never that anything is right. render_probe_knowledge and render_probe_search PASS with 0 page errors.

Verified visually, not only by probe: Ask Wallach returns the question as BEST ANSWER under WHAT TO DO with the plain short answer, the plain full answer and the byte-exact quote; the B9 element card posts 'WALLACH DAILY TARGET 1,000 mcg'. That screenshot also carries an outside corroboration of the ruling -- every top Youngevity folate source exceeds 1,000 mcg (ReVERSE! 1,333 mcg, 3.0 Rise & Restore 1,400 mcg, Ultimate Cardio FX 1,360 mcg). Under the old 400 mcg target ReVERSE! would have posted 333% of target. Youngevity composition corroborates here; it never supplied the number.

One trap corrected for the future: memory mining-mechanics section 7 listed epigenetics and search-enrichment.json as indent=2. Both measure indent=1 today, and lets-play-doctor is now the ONLY indent=2 draft. Writing on the memorised list would have silently reformatted two pillars into tens of thousands of diff lines and buried the real change. The staging script refused to write unless an indent in 1..4 reproduced the file byte-exactly, which is the rule printed directly beside the wrong list. The rule held; the data next to it did not.

summary: Editing one sentence rewrote a whole book file: mine_batch hardcoded indent=2 while 6 of 7 pillars are indent=1, so a 2-line change shipped inside 40,000 lines of whitespace. Both writers now preserve the indent they find.
detail:
This one is worth remembering because the safeguard existed and still did not work.

The project's notes have carried a warning since July: the seven book files are not all stored the same way -- some use one space of indentation, one uses two -- so always MEASURE a file's spacing before saving it, never assume. That warning is aimed at a human. The tool that applies claim edits was hardcoded to save at two spaces. So when it edited a single sentence in one claim, it re-spaced all 512 claims in Let's Play Doctor on the way out, and the sealing step faithfully copied that re-spacing into the sealed file. The data was never wrong. But the actual change -- two lines -- was now buried in forty thousand lines of whitespace, and a change nobody can review is not really reviewable just because it is correct.

The lesson is the section 00.B one, demonstrated rather than argued: a rule written in a memory binds whoever reads the memory. It does not bind a tool. The tool had been quietly breaking the rule for weeks while the rule sat there being true.

TECHNICAL RECORD. mine_batch.py:154 and corpus_extract.py:208 both hardcoded json.dumps(..., indent=2). Measured at HEAD: the lets-play-doctor shard and draft were BOTH indent=1 before this session, so mine_batch's write flipped 1 -> 2, and corpus_seal.py:148 -- which promotes by copying the draft's own bytes (target.write_text(lf_text(d))) -- carried the reformat onto the golden-protected shard. git diff --stat showed 20,000 insertions and 20,000 deletions around one claim_text edit.

Fix: mine_batch gained _detect_indent(raw, doc, path), which tries indent 1..4, requires byte-exact reproduction of the file it just read, and RAISES SystemExit rather than guessing; the write now uses that value. corpus_extract detects the SHARD's indent with the same probe, since finalize rebuilds the draft from the shard. mine_batch selftest passes all 11 cases.

Repair: rewrote the draft at indent=1 through safe_write, asserting afterwards that the claim_text edit survived the reformat, then re-sealed. corpus_seal is USER-ONLY on EVERY invocation -- the authorisation given earlier in this same session did not carry, so it was asked again and granted again. Sealed kv=460, 2254 claims, corpus_verify PASS. The diff for claims-lets-play-doctor.json collapsed from 40,000 lines to 2 (1 insertion, 1 deletion); claims-epigenetics.json is 41 deletions, the purged folate claim. This CORRECTS the preceding build-log line and Creator's Log entry, both of which recorded kv=459.

Re-verified after the re-seal, not assumed from the earlier run: build_embeds 15/15 artifacts, build.mjs exit 0, invariants 88/88 with 0 failed and no new reds (23 external / 23 consistency / 40 structural / 2 meta), render_probe_knowledge and render_probe_search PASS with 0 page errors.

Two things deliberately NOT done, flagged rather than silently skipped. First, corpus_extract.py:208 still writes with draft_path.write_text instead of routing through safe_write, which is a section 17 violation in its own right; it is a separate defect and needs its own decision rather than being folded into a folate round. Second, no invariant was added for indent stability: there is no declared expected indent per pillar to gate against, and inventing one unilaterally would ship a WISH dressed as a gate, which R7 forbids. The honest position is that the WRITERS are now correct and nothing yet PROVES they stay correct.

summary: Cross-book comparison is banned from ALL presentation, not just contradictions -- 'all books agree' included. It was live: 5 of 6 shipped header why-lines ended with an earlier-book clause. Truncated; magnesium was already clean.
detail:
Yesterday Luneth said to stop putting book contradictions in front of readers. I took that narrowly, as being about disagreements. He corrected the scope today, and the correction is the interesting part: showing that the books AGREE is just as bad, and in one way worse. Announcing "all his books agree on this" quietly tells a reader that sometimes they don't. Nobody asked. It is our internal business leaking onto the page.

The worst version is the one that lists exceptions -- "they all say it except these two, which leave it out." That does two bad things at once: it exposes that Wallach changed his mind over the years, and it invents a meaning for the omission that he never stated. And the deepest version is any line that tells the reader HOW WE CHOSE, like "the app favors the newest Wallach number." The reader should never learn there is a rule.

The rule now: say what the newest claim says, and stop. Naming one book as the source is provenance and stays. Putting two books in relation is the violation.

What made this urgent is that it was not a demo problem. It was already shipping. Five of the six live element headers ended their "why this number" note with a comparison to an older book. Magnesium -- the most recent one shipped -- was the only clean one, which suggests the habit was being trained out naturally and nobody noticed the older five still had it.

TECHNICAL RECORD. dashboard/assets/data/entity-copy.json is hand_authored (an R4 prose home, per eden/derived/MANIFEST.json -- checked before editing, because being listed in the MANIFEST does not mean it is derived). CRLF, indent=2, both established by byte-exact round-trip; the writer refuses if no indent 1..4 reproduces the file. Truncated the trailing clause on calcium, selenium, copper, zinc and vitamin-a; asserted magnesium untouched and asserted afterwards that no why-line anywhere contains 'earlier', a year, 'supersedes', or 'favors the newest'.

This was an audit, not a spot-fix. Every front-facing block of all 40 demo pages was scanned with a 10-pattern matcher that deliberately skips citation-ish spans (a chip naming one book and year is provenance and must survive), plus a separate scan of the live prose stores. 28 flagged blocks across 17 demo pages, of which 5 are panels whose entire concept IS the comparison.

VERIFICATION, including one instrument that lied. build.mjs 0; invariants 88/88, 0 failed, no new reds (23 external / 23 consistency / 40 structural / 2 meta); render_probe_entity PASS, 0 page errors, and it independently reports calcium's whyTipText as the truncated string. My first check reported 'mentionsOtherBook: false' for every header -- which was worthless, because the why-line is a HOVER tooltip (.kd-ep-why > .kd-ep-tip) that had never rendered. An absence proves nothing when the thing was never present. The rerun reads the tip from the DOM with tipPresent=true as a negative control FIRST, and only then trusts the negative.

HONEST LIMIT: the tooltip's text is verified from the live DOM, but headless hover would not paint the tooltip, so no pixels of the popup were inspected. It took three iterations and every failure was a REFUSE guard firing rather than a mangled file: cobalt used div+p+cite, germanium had inline style= after the class, vitamin-b6 used a bare

RESEARCH, because two of his notes were questions rather than instructions. Niacin panel G: he doubted normal people have any of its self-diagnosis signs. TWO HONEST LIMITS recorded rather than glossed, because he asked me to check IF the stance is really Wallach's. First, he attacks the FEAR of skin cancer and what it caused, never the oncology -- no claim in any book says skin cancer from sun is unreal or overstated, so that argument cannot be built without fabricating it. Second, he is on BOTH sides of sunscreen: DDDL-000144 (2011) recommends it for preventing sunburn. summary: Swept all 2,250 claims for more superseded dose ceilings after yesterday's vitamin D deletions. Found exactly one survivor -- and it did not need deleting. Zero claims removed.
detail:
Yesterday three claims were deleted for telling readers to cap vitamin D at 400 IU a day, against the 1,000-2,000 IU his newest book gives. This was the obvious follow-up: how many more are hiding? The answer turned out to be one, and the honest fix was not deletion. The claim summarised a whole page of the book but only quoted the bottom of it, and the bad number lived in the un-quoted part -- so trimming the summary back to what its own quote actually says removed the 400 IU limit without losing a single word Wallach really wrote. A second claim looked identical and was the exact opposite: its quote had been cut too SHORT, and trimming it would have destroyed a real angina protocol. That one got its full passage back instead.

WHAT THE SWEEP ACTUALLY DID. 2,250 claims, four overlapping passes: a wide net for ceiling language (485), a tightening to bound-word-near-a-number (57, all read), an entity-anchored pass requiring the bound word to GOVERN a named essential (120, all read), and every contraindication and toxicity_sign read regardless (73). Plus a complete enumeration of all 50 vitamin-D claims. Both detectors were negative-controlled against the three already-deleted claims: 3/3 caught. The first entity pass was thrown away -- it scored 461 with 'histidine' on top, because the canon stores the 3-letter amino abbreviation and 'His' matched every 'His treatment...'. That is the same stemming noise the last session recorded, hit again from a new angle.

THE RESULT, AND WHY IT IS SMALL. Only one numeric ceiling in the whole corpus still sits below its essential's current target. Two other candidates dissolved on reading: one is a deficiency FLOOR, not a ceiling, and the other attributes its 15 mcg selenium limit to Pauling and refutes it in the same breath. There is a structural reason the list is this short, and it is checkable rather than a hunch: nearly every 1995-to-2014 target moved DOWN (molybdenum 500 to 10-25 mcg, vanadium 500 to 50-100, iron 45 to 15-30). Vitamin D is the only essential whose number rose sharply. An old ceiling can only contradict a new target when the target went UP, so vitamin D was structurally the only place this could happen at all.

A DECISION I HAD TO REVERSE MID-TASK. I presented the angina claim as the same prose-overreach defect and Luneth approved trimming it. Then reading the book at its offset showed the entire ANGINA entry sitting immediately before the quoted slice -- the write-up was faithful and the QUOTE was too narrow. Trimming would have deleted chelation-over-bypass, calcium 2,000 mg, magnesium 800 mg, EFA and hawthorn to remove a numberless sentence we are keeping in another claim anyway. I stopped and re-asked rather than executing the approved-but-now-wrong instruction, and he chose to widen.

A TOOL THAT WAS ABOUT TO WRECK A FILE. vb_apply.py had indent=2 hardcoded while the draft it edits is indent=1. One verbatim edit would have re-spaced all 510 claims, and the seal would have promoted that reformat onto the golden shard -- burying a 2-line change in roughly 40,000. That is the identical failure fixed in two sibling tools on 2026-08-05; this one was missed. It now measures before writing, and measures BEFORE mutating (afterwards the original bytes cannot be reproduced). Actual sealed-shard diff for both claim edits: 3 insertions, 4 deletions.

The per-book indent list in memory was wrong again, in a third direction. Measured: lets-play-doctor is indent=1, not the sole indent=2. Three drafts reproduce at no indent at all, because they are indent=1 with CRLF while the check compares LF-joined output -- both sanctioned edit tools will now refuse to write those three. The refusal is correct and fail-safe; the message was misleading, so it now names CRLF when it sees it.

A GATE THAT WENT RED BECAUSE OF THE FIX. Widening the angina quote made it span five OCR line-wrap hyphens the short slice was too small to contain, so frontface_verbatims_clean reddened. That is the documented trap -- on a post-fix red, ask what was making it pass before. The answer was 'the quote was too small to contain the defect'. Fixed at source, scoped to that span only, CRLF preserved, and 'coronary by-pass' deliberately left because it is the book's real mid-line hyphenation rather than a wrap.

WHAT I AM NOT CLAIMING. The board is 89/89 and that means nothing drifted, not that anything is right -- 23 of the 89 gates bear on truth outside our own files. render_probe_search fails, and I proved it was already failing at HEAD by stashing the whole working tree and re-running it there, rather than assuming. The sweep also surfaced a larger defect class I did NOT fix: at least 86 claims state a figure in their write-up that is absent from their own quote. 86 is a floor with a known false-negative mode -- my own counter wrongly cleared the vitamin D claim, because it tolerates twice-daily halving and 400 matched the 200 inside '75-200 mg'. No gate was written, because the rule needs Luneth's call on legitimate restatement versus overreach, and inventing it would be a WISH dressed as a gate.

One coverage hole is named rather than hidden: with the twin deleted and this one trimmed, the corpus now carries no heart-disease PREVENTION protocol, only post-heart-attack treatment.

summary: Swept every open corpus defect class at once after Luneth found duplicate cards on the vitamin D page. Root cause: the duplicate gate is blind three ways. 46 re-filed, 20 deleted, 2 fabricated doses caught.
detail:
Luneth pointed at two cards on the vitamin D page saying the same thing and asked why duplicates keep surviving pass after pass. He was right to be angry, and the honest answer is that the gate meant to catch them could never have seen them. It compares claims only within the same book, only within the same section of a page, and only when one quote is a literal substring of the other. Two books wording the same fact differently miss all three tests. Every previous pass was fixing symptoms one at a time against a detector that was structurally blind.

So this time nothing was fixed one at a time. Agents read the actual book pages for 1,021 candidate pairs, 71 same-source groups, 88 suspect figures and every OCR fusion in seven books, and every proposed deletion was handed to a second agent whose only job was to refute it.

THE RESULT WAS THE OPPOSITE OF WHAT I EXPECTED. Almost nothing needed deleting. 396 of 406 cross-book pairs and 508 of 615 cross-facet pairs came back genuinely different claims. The real defect was that claims were filed under the wrong section heading, so unrelated claims ended up side by side looking like copies. And the reason for THAT turned out to be a design flaw rather than sloppy authoring: the colour family literally named 'signs' contains only 'warning', so anyone filing a deficiency SIGN is pulled toward it, while the correct home sits in the 'science' family. Worse, 'warning' is pinned second on the page, so the misfiled claim gets promoted ABOVE its correct twin. That is mechanically why those two cards ended up next to each other on his screen.

I deliberately did NOT build the obvious gate. Forcing one facet per claim kind would demand 941 re-facets, 41.8% of the corpus, and would be wrong: a 'definition' claim legitimately spans thirteen facets, because 'Where does niobium get its name?' and 'Where is sulfur stored in the body?' are the same kind and belong in different sections. A gate that has to be wrong 941 times to be satisfied is not a gate, it is a wish with teeth.

TWO CLAIMS WERE STATING DOSES THAT ARE NOWHERE IN THE BOOK THEY CITE. Not invented -- contaminated. One asserted selenium at 1,000-3,000 mcg a day and displayed that figure in its reader-facing answer; an exhaustive search of all 1.17 million characters of Rare Earths found it zero times, and found it instead in Dead Doctors. The other asserted chromium's body burden and a USDA prevalence figure absent from all 692,000 characters of Hell's Kitchen and present in four other books. Both are real Wallach, attributed to the wrong source. Both trimmed.

I CORRUPTED SIX DOSE NUMBERS MYSELF AND CAUGHT IT BEFORE IT SHIPPED. Joining OCR line-break hyphens in the newly widened quotes, my pattern matched digits as well as letters, so '800-\n1200' collapsed into '8001200' across six vitamin E doses, plus two vitamin B designations and two year ranges. The project's own gate pattern is letters-only; I had written a looser one. I found it by reading what the script actually did rather than trusting that it worked, reverted the book sources through git, and re-ran it with the pattern narrowed to match the gate. Nothing reached a seal. This is precisely the class the source rule exists to prevent, and it was my error, not one I inherited.

The guards earned their keep repeatedly. A tool refused an entire book rather than orphan a mapped condition. My own sync guard aborted rather than silently overwrite 57 corrected quotes with the older narrower ones. The OCR sweep skipped Asa Chandler and thirteen instances of Kazuhiko Asai that a naive replace would have mangled. And after the deletions a gate found a THIRD place a claim id can live -- a hand-authored mechanism file where selenium's rendered quote pointed at a claim I had just removed. The standing lesson said a purge is two deletions. It is three.

Board 89/89, corpus sealed at 469, 2,230 claims, three seals all authorised individually. Still open and named rather than buried: 46 more question collisions across 93 claims, which is the same twin-card symptom corpus-wide and now has a workflow running against it.

summary: Shipped no_duplicate_questions (board 89 -> 90): two claims on one entity page can no longer ask the reader the same thing. Threshold-free, 29 known cases allowlisted in-gate with reasons that expire.
detail:
The duplicate cards Luneth kept finding now have a machine that catches them, which is the only thing that actually ends this. Every previous pass fixed instances; the class survived because the detector was structurally blind to it.

WHAT THE GATE ASKS. Not "are these claims similar?" -- that needs judgement and a threshold, and both drift. It asks the one question that is decidable: do two claims on the same entity page ask the reader the same thing? Bucket by subject and normalised question; a bucket with more than one claim is a violation. Normalisation lowercases, strips punctuation, drops a small stopword list and sorts the remaining tokens, so a reordered restatement still collides while genuinely different content words do not. No score, no tuning, nothing to drift.

WHY A SECOND GATE INSTEAD OF FIXING THE FIRST. no_duplicate_claims puts the book inside its bucket key and additionally demands that one quote literally contain the other. Measured today, it cannot see 407 cross-book and 615 cross-facet candidate pairs. The vitamin D pair Luneth found by eye was invisible to it three separate ways.

WHAT I REFUSED TO BUILD, AND WHY. The facet audit recommended extending the old gate to compare claims across facets inside one book. I measured that before accepting it: 28 pairs, and most are the legitimate pattern where one paragraph correctly answers a "What is X?" and a "What does X do?", or a catalog entry correctly feeds both a discovery and an etymology card. A gate that fires on 28 correct cases is noise, and noise trains people to ignore the board. Recommendation overridden on evidence, and the reasoning is written into the gate's own comment so nobody re-proposes it from the audit next month.

THE ALLOWLIST HAD TO EXPIRE. 29 known collisions remain, and Luneth wants them cleared next session, so the gate ships with them listed. The dangerous version of that is a baseline entry, which is invariant-scoped and would forgive the entire class forever. Instead each group sits inside the gate with a written reason of one of two kinds: no honest split exists (one claim is a strict content subset of the other, or it is the same Wallach passage reprinted in two books), or it is genuinely distinct but its short answer must be re-cut before its question can move. And a carve-out that stops matching FAILS the gate -- so fixing a collision forces deleting its excuse in the same patch. The list cannot rot into an amnesty.

That second category is the lesson from earlier today worth keeping. An agent can always invent a question that sounds distinct; 25 of 44 proposed re-cuts promised content that was in neither the answer nor the claim. Shipping those would have replaced a duplicate-looking card with one that lies about what it answers, which is strictly worse. So the rule is now explicit: a question its own card cannot answer is a worse defect than the duplicate it replaces.

The negative test runs seven cases and the one I care most about is the one where the gate must NOT fire: the same question under two different subjects renders on two different pages and is not a duplicate. Two of the seven cases were wrong when I first wrote them -- one raised a TypeError because ** demands string keys, and one reused a real question that collided with an unrelated third zinc claim, a test bug wearing a gate bug's clothes. Both are fixed with the reason recorded in the file rather than quietly corrected.

Board 90/90. Corpus untouched this round -- no seal, still 2,230 claims at version 469. Everything else Luneth listed is deferred to the next session by his instruction, so nothing hangs over the header demo work when we return to it.

summary: Set up the duplicate-removal campaign properly: a deterministic detector (274 candidate pairs) + an offline dashboard where Luneth rules keep/merge/not-dup per pair. Nothing deleted without his say-so; apply step runs next session against his exported decisions.
detail:
Closing out the session that rebuilt the duplicate-removal work after the 2026-08-06 rollback. This time the process IS the product: a machine finds likely-duplicate pairs, and Luneth personally rules on every one before anything is deleted.

Detector — tools/dedup/find_duplicate_candidates.py: deterministic, no LLM in the path, every pair tagged with the signal(s) that caught it plus a transparent score. Six signals: same_question, verbatim_same_section / cross_facet / cross_book, span_overlap_same_book (tightened to overlap >= 60% of the LONGER span, from 50%-of-shorter, to drop the legitimate multi-facet-mining false positives), text_near_same_subject, verbatim_reprint (full-string ratio). Cross-subject token similarity deliberately excluded — Wallach writes the same sentence shape per nutrient (copper~iron, phenylalanine~valine score ~1.0 but are different entities); genuine cross-subject reuse is caught by full-string reprint instead. 274 candidate pairs at kv466.

Dashboard — tools/dedup/review.html + review-data.js: offline, self-contained, user-approved after a screenshot review. One pair at a time, both claims in full, signals/score/prior-ruling shown; rulings keep-A / keep-B / merge / not-a-duplicate plus a note; resumable via localStorage; exports dedup-decisions.json. Verified headless (0 pageerrors) and the full rule -> persist -> export path exercised then reset clean. Committed 01d24629 on branch duplicate-review-campaign (local only).

Also this session: opened PR #1 (protocol-widen, kv469) on master; fast-forwarded origin/master ece492f7 -> be7a2d51 so the PR base was correct; deleted the cancelled derive-counts branch and the stale claude/nervous-shannon branch (local + remote); rewrote next-chunk.md to lead with the apply step.

Next session: Luneth attaches dedup-decisions.json; build and run the apply step — keep-one deletes the other claim plus its enrichment, re-derives the indices, and reseals (user-authorized); merge authors the combined claim for his approval first; not-a-duplicate does nothing. Guardrail: apply ONLY the rulings in the file — no re-facet, no un-enrich, no scope creep (that is what caused the rollback). Board 89/89, corpus untouched at kv466.

summary: Rebased PR #1 (protocol-widen) onto the post-dedup master: replayed its 38 dose-widenings + 2 book de-hyphenations byte-exact on kv467, re-sealed kv468, board 89/89. PR #1 can now merge without conflicts.
detail:
PR #1 (protocol-widen-batch) widened 38 protocol quotes to capture their doses and de-hyphenated the OCR wraps it exposed. It was based on the pre-dedup corpus (kv469 off the rollback), so after the dedup landed on master (kv467) it could no longer merge. This session rebased it.

detail:
A productive stretch on the element-header collection. After Vitamin D finally landed earlier this session, three more sets went the same clean-slate way — build four (or six) genuinely distinct, beautiful concept mockups, trust the freed-up design skill instead of the old static-diagram rules, and let Luneth pick. WHAT WAS BUILT (all demo-only, parked in temporary/awaiting-refinement/, nothing shipped live)
- Vitamin K (4 concepts): A "Two Jobs" (the seal-a-wound / cement-calcium-into-bone diptych), B "Homemade Half" (you brew about half your K in your own gut), C "Read the Bruise" (easy bruising as a readable sign, kept honest as "K or E"), D "Activator X" (Weston Price's lost butter factor, K2 kept hedged). "All 4 good."
- Vitamin B12 (6 concepts): A "Red Crystal" (a cobalt-cored red gem in a dark jewel-box — his favourite), B "Made by Microbes" (the soil-to-you supply chain of a vitamin you can't make), C "What Survives" (how much B12 cooking and processing destroy), D "Losing the Insulation" (demyelination). Then, at his push, the ENERGY angle most people actually associate with B12: E "Why B12 energises you" (it builds the red cells that carry oxygen) and F "Why you're secretly low" (the absorption gauntlet - stomach acid, intrinsic factor, gut). The energy panels took three tries: the first pass explained the mechanism but led with a debunk and fell flat; the fix was to lead with the visceral "oh, so THIS is why" and give them punchy, personal headlines.
- Iron (4 concepts, the first MINERAL set - blue accent instead of orange): A "the seat oxygen rides" (oxygen clips onto iron; carbon monoxide steals the same seat 200x tighter), B "the body screaming for iron" (pica - craving ice, dirt, paint - backed by a real 11-of-13 vs 3-of-12 trial), C "the metal that built us" (earth's molten-iron core to the few grams in your blood), D "it was never the iron" (his favourite: excess iron isn't the poison, it burns through your selenium, copper and zinc). He expects the final iron header to be some combination of all four.

SOURCE DISCIPLINE (section 00.A)
Every displayed quote is byte-exact from a sealed book, pulled by claim-id. The recurring trap this pack made vivid: the best-sounding facts often live only in a claim's claim_text, never its verbatim - "myelin," "deposition of calcium in bones," B12's soil ppm thresholds, iron's Iron Age and "90% of metal." Those all stayed in my own words as grounded gloss, never in quotation marks. Popular framings ("energy drink") are flagged as our editorial voice, never put in Wallach's mouth. Two deliberate anti-repeats: iron's oxygen story was built around the iron seat + the CO twist so it wouldn't echo B12; and the "metal at the centre of chlorophyll" identity was avoided entirely, since the Magnesium header and B12's red gem already spend it.

METHOD NOTES
Each set: read the grounded dossier, pull verbatims by id, build self-contained fragments (bespoke CSS + light animation + fixed-px SVG art so declared pixels stay screen pixels), render in the real container via mockup_harness, measure (every figure scale 1.000, zero text collisions), screenshot every panel, park at depth-2 in awaiting-refinement. - B (Luneth favourite) "What burns your food": the furnace — carbohydrate + fat + protein converge along animated flow-lines into a glowing NAD·NADP core that radiates Energy to the right; the core glow-pulses. Anchor WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000037 (the pack's only mechanism claim).
- C (Luneth favourite) "Why time-release?": the niacin flush — a "big dose all at once" panel flaring a warm bloom vs a "time-release" panel staying calm, over the insight that Wallach writes "time-release" on nearly every niacin dose. The 18 mg government RDA inside LETS-000059 is deliberately never surfaced (the figure Wallach reprints only to argue against). - D "The dose ladder": four climbing rungs — 50 mg maintenance floor, 100 mg daily target, 200–500 mg short-term therapeutic, and the surprise top rung, 500 mg that "repels mosquitoes" (a little mosquito glyph). Anchor WAL-CLM-LETS-000068 (50 & 200–500 mg) + WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000112 (10–100 mg → 100) + WAL-CLM-LETS-000370 (the mosquito curio).

summary: Built B6's five header-demo concepts; Luneth rejected all - not the info, the presentation. Nothing banked; rebuilding fresh. Rule audit he asked for: NO restrictive rule caused it - the visuals drifted to infographic/diagram idioms instead of beautiful heroes.
detail:
Built five header-demo concepts for vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) and Luneth rejected all of them. His words: "clearly lower quality than the rest ... the info isn't necessarily the issue, it's the way it's presented." Nothing was banked or shipped; B6 will be rebuilt fresh in a new session. This entry records the miss and the honest audit he asked for.

What the five were (temporary/header-fragments/vb6-frags/ + temporary/awaiting-refinement/vitamin-b6-demos-r1.html): A a two-danger-zone dose dial, B an epilepsy twin-EEG hero, C a drug-drain reservoir with a 15-20% stat, D a three-stage pregnancy timeline, E a carpal-tunnel surgery-vs-vitamin swap.

Diagnosis (a diagnosis, not a rule): the visuals drifted into infographic / diagram idioms — a labelled dose gauge, a stat plus a draining vessel, a numbered timeline, comparison cards — instead of the singular, beautiful, often typographic or organic HERO images that made the two approved sets land: niacin (three monumental letterform Ds, a glowing NAD/NADP furnace) and B1 (the heart-to-mind poles, the rice-grain cross-sections). The B6 pieces were competent diagrams, not beautiful heroes. Effort was also spread thin across five concepts. Separately, the epilepsy concept deviated to an oversized 1.42rem pull-quote; the standard bordered ~1.04rem quote is byte-identical to niacin and B1, so only that one concept broke the consistent quote treatment.

Rule audit (Luneth explicitly asked whether a rule made between the last good demo and this one caused the regression, and to reveal it if so): NO restrictive rule was made. No memory file, skill, or CLAUDE.md was changed this session. The only writes between the B1 demo (approved) and the B6 demo (rejected) were the B1 round-close records (build-log, creators-log) and handoff bookkeeping (adding the B1 entry to next-chunk and removing B1 from the remaining-dossiers list) — all visible in git. The one design-relevant note added earlier (during the B3 round-close, in next-chunk: "give every figure a HERO moment — a boxed loop / bar chart / stat-tile dashboard reads boring/clinical") is pro-ambition and argues against the very clinical drift that happened, so this was a failure to heed my own note, not a restriction imposed on me.

Grounding was clean regardless: all 12 non-dead cited claim-ids verified live; the dossier-drift dead id RARE-000237 was substituted with the live EPIGEN-000108 + LETS-000027; every pull-quote was byte-exact. Board 90/90; build exit 0.

Retry, next session: rebuild B6 fresh, pushing each concept toward a striking hero with real craft (the verified grounding and concept material are preserved in chronicle/next-chunk.md). Do not ban any shape — per the vitamin-D header postmortem, diagnose causes, don't ban shapes — and do not add restrictive rules, per Luneth's standing instruction.

summary: Correction: I wrongly told Luneth I didn't change the quote styling - he proved a before/after. My demos (niacin, B1, B6) dropped the app's real .ds-pull-quote component for a plain border-left quote; my 'no change' compared to an already-regressed baseline. Record corrected.
detail:
A correction to the record, and to what I told Luneth. He asked why I changed the quote styling in B6; I answered that I hadn't — that the standard quote was byte-identical to niacin and B1 and only the epilepsy concept deviated. He then showed a before/after screenshot proving I had changed it. He was right. This entry corrects the falsehood I stated and committed (the prior B6-rejection note, entry lg_mskw09hw_pcfv52).

The truth: the established Wallach-quote treatment is the app's design-system component `.ds-pull-quote` — a large italic pull-quote carrying the giant opening-quote glyph (via ::before, in the accent colour), a `.ds-mark` warm-yellow highlight on the key phrase, a `footer` attribution reading "— DR. JOEL WALLACH · BOOK (ED. YEAR)", plus a "General education, not medical advice" disclaimer. It is rendered live by entity-page.ts and defined in design-system.css (.ds-mark at line 475, .ds-pull-quote at 749), documented in STYLE-GUIDE.md.

My header demos — niacin, B1, and B6, and the mineral run before them — hand-rolled a plain border-left quote at about 1.04rem with a mono claim-id line, instead of that component. That is a real and visible regression.

Why my answer was false, mechanically: I compared B6's quote only against niacin's and B1's. But those two had already abandoned .ds-pull-quote, so "byte-identical to niacin/B1" measured against an already-regressed baseline and confirmed a falsehood rather than catching it. Comparing to the wrong baseline is how I convinced myself nothing had changed.

Fixes applied this session: corrected chronicle/next-chunk.md (the B6-retry note's quote diagnosis had it backwards — the plain quote IS the regression, not the standard) and appended a correction line to chronicle/build-log.md. No fragment files were reverted (all gitignored scratch; niacin and B1 remain banked as starting points, with the quote fix now logged as a refinement item for them too).

Deeper lesson, and probably the real root of the "lower quality" Luneth flagged beyond the infographic-idioms point: build header figures with the real design-system components, not hand-rolled approximations of them. The retry, and the eventual refinement of niacin and B1, must use the real .ds-pull-quote + .ds-mark treatment.

summary: B2 header approved at round 4 after three rejections. The lesson: a header figure must LABEL ITS OWN PARTS -- unlabelled mood art "literally says nothing". Found it by screenshotting the sets Luneth had already approved, instead of designing from taste a fourth time.
detail:
Vitamin B2's illustrated header took four attempts. The first three were rejected, and the third
rejection is the one that taught something. I had built five figures that were genuinely beautiful -- a field
of lights guttering out, a crack splitting open, a glare washing out a room, a fluorescent glow breathing in
the dark -- and Luneth threw all five out: "huge illustrations that literally say nothing ... it's there for
no apparent reason. Illustrations MUST MAKE VISUAL SENSE." He was right. Every one of those figures was an
atmosphere with no words in it; all the explaining sat in the text underneath, so the picture itself carried
nothing. Rather than guess a fourth time, I opened the header sets he had already approved and looked at what
they had in common. It was not subtle: every approved figure names its parts inside the frame. So the fourth
round rebuilt all six figures that way, and he picked three of them.

WHAT WAS REJECTED AND WHY (r3, five concepts, all deleted)
Unlabelled atmospheres: a dot-field "cell lights" wave, an abstract fissure, an optical glare bloom, a
luminous whey glow, plus one typographic roster. Four of the five carried zero in-figure text; every label sat
below the figure, disconnected. Diagnosis in Luneth's words: they "say nothing" and are "there for no apparent
reason."

THE RULE, DERIVED FROM EVIDENCE NOT TASTE
Screenshotted temporary/awaiting-refinement/vitamin-b3-demos-r1.html and vitamin-b1-demos-r1.html. Niacin's
NAD figure labels Carbohydrate / Fat / Protein going in and Energy coming out. B1's rice grain labels
"thiamine-bearing bran" on a leader line, "POLISHING" on the arrow, and captions each grain. Niacin's three Ds
label each letter with its word plus THE GUT / THE SKIN / THE MIND. The falsifiable test that falls out:
could a reader get the whole panel from the figure alone, with the prose removed? If no, it is decoration.
Corollary: he does NOT dislike diagrams -- the standing "diagram clutter" failure mode is about CLUTTER; a
clean 5-node labelled flow is the approved genre. Also: restrained line art on the tan background, not 760px
dark full-bleed slabs.

r4 -- SIX LABELLED CONCEPTS, THREE PICKED
A what B2 becomes (B2 -> FMN + FAD -> Energy under named columns) - B it switches the others on (two named
conversions: inactive B6 -> functional B6, tryptophan -> niacin, each enzyme named on its arrow; NEW this
round and the strongest unused idea) - C the three sites Wallach names, three across, each mark over its own
name - D his 12-entry deficiency roster with depression and dizziness ignited - E the 1879 discovery: a dish
of whey and its fluorescence, both labelled, over an 1879/1932/1935 rule - F clear lens vs clouded lens with
the early eye signs named. Luneth: "C, E and F are the best."

DEFECTS CAUGHT BY LOOKING, THAT NO PROBE REPORTS
(1) a leader line running straight through its own caption -- the single most common rejection in this project
-- fixed by rebuilding C as a three-across roster that needs no leaders at all; (2) a caption clipped at the
SVG edge; (3) a caption whose last word sat behind a drawn vessel. All three were invisible to the text-vs-text
collision pass and visible immediately in a screenshot.

DOSSIER DRIFT -- SECOND CONFIRMED CASE
chronicle/header-research/vitamin-b2.md carries two flags that are now false: it says the mechanism lives in
claim_text with "no mechanism verbatim to pull by ID" (WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000243 has a full quotable one, used in
four panels), and it says the yellow-green pigment fact is world knowledge that must never be injected
(WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000297 states it byte-exact, plus 1932 Warburg / 1935 Kuhn). Concept E -- one of his three
picks -- is built entirely on grounding the dossier forbids. The same pattern then appeared in vitamin-b5.md
(says 10 claims, there are 17; declares a discovery/history concept unsupported when WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000253 is
exactly that). Two in a row is a pattern, not a coincidence; flagged for a sweep.

TOOLING -- A HOLE CLOSED
tools/mockup_measure.js compared text against text only, so it passed a figure whose label read "sterols and
steroid hormone|s" -- nothing overlapped it, it simply ran off the canvas. It now also checks every label
against its own viewBox edges (right/left/bottom) and exits non-zero on a clip. Proved the check can fire
before trusting it: reports "CLIPPED LABELS: none" on the fixed page and fires on a deliberately clipped
control label. Board 90/90 after the change.

FILES
temporary/awaiting-refinement/vitamin-b2-demos-r4.html (6 panels) + temporary/header-fragments/vb2-frags/
(6 fragments); r1 + r3 and eight orphaned fragments moved to
temporary/recycling-bin/_superseded/2026-08-09-vb2-rejected-rounds/ (moved, not deleted). tools/mockup_measure.js
gains the clipped-label check. chronicle/next-chunk.md banks B2 r4 and records the labelled-figure rule and the
dossier drift. Memory element-header-illustration-failure-modes.md gains the rule as its top section.

VERIFICATION
6 figures at scale 1.000; zero label-box overlaps by a getBBox probe (mockup_measure's residual flags are
stacked two-line captions, confirmed non-overlapping); scroll proven by a real wheel event; every verbatim
pulled by claim id at generation time with a hard failure on a missing slice, never hand-typed. Board 90/90
(23 external / 24 consistency / 41 structural / 2 meta) -- nothing drifted, which is not the same as anything
being right. Build parity fresh.

IN FLIGHT, NOT CLOSED
B5 (pantothenic acid) r1 is built -- six labelled concepts -- and is awaiting Luneth's picks. It is deliberately
not part of this round-close.

summary: B5 header approved (5 of 6 concepts) · a dashboard that answers "which nutrient is most responsible" without inventing the number Wallach never wrote · and a sweep proving the research dossiers are systemically stale: 25 of 47 cite dead claim ids, 44 of 47 undercount themselves.
detail:
Three pieces of work closed together, and the third is the one that matters most.

B5 (PANTOTHENIC ACID) -- FIVE OF SIX CONCEPTS PICKED
The labelled-figure rule learned from B2 held on the first attempt: six concepts, five approved
("A, C, D, E, and F are all good"). A becomes-coenzyme-A (B5 -> CoA -> four unrelated jobs under
named columns) - C body-vs-mood, the same deficiency list split into two lanes, every word his -
D four doses drawn to one scale, the 4 mg RDA as a sliver, with a 100x hero to the overdose range -
E found-by-accident, a labelled yeast flask and 1930s->1940 - F the quiet teammate, four programs
at a near-constant dose. B (three books, one shared sign) was NOT picked, and the reason is worth
keeping: "showing contradictions across books is not something to bring front-facing." The figure
was built to show three books AGREEING on burning feet; he read it as three books disagreeing. He
said explicitly not to make a rule of it, so it is recorded as a note.

Two factual slips were caught before he saw them, both corrected toward the more conservative
reading. D's headline claimed you would need "five thousand times" the RDA before Wallach calls it
an overdose; his range is 10-20 g, so it BEGINS at 2,500x -- 5,000x is the top of the range, and
putting the threshold there overstates how much is safe. In a dose context that is exactly where
00.A demands rigidity. C claimed burning feet sits "four words" from quarrelsome; the verbatim
gives three.

THE OVERLAP DASHBOARD -- ANSWERING AN UNANSWERABLE QUESTION HONESTLY
Luneth noticed that many nutrients share deficiency signs (depression, mood) and worried a header
would imply "THIS is the mood vitamin". He asked which nutrients are MOST responsible for which
conditions, on a percentage scale, and flagged himself that this might not be derivable without
hallucinating. He was right: Wallach assigns no percentage of responsibility to any nutrient for
any condition, anywhere in the seven books. Inventing one would have been fabrication.

So the dashboard derives the only thing that IS in the corpus -- how often he says it. Share of
Wallach's own claims for a condition, split into cause (deficiency_sign) and cure (protocol),
never summed, with book-breadth offered as the more honest signal. The distinction is stated in
the largest type on the page.

The headline finding is deflating and useful: only 11 of 542 conditions have three or more
INDEPENDENT claims on both sides. Everywhere else a single protocol claim names a dozen nutrients
at once and all of them score, so a "ranking" is really a membership list -- 356 of 365 cards say
so explicitly, with the count of distinct source claims per lane. Least-specific signs: arthritis
45 nutrients, depression 31, headache 31, rheumatoid arthritis 30, dementia 28. Luneth's instinct
was right and the problem is wider than mood. Design consequence: no header may imply one element
owns a crowded sign. Verified by writing an independent recount of depression and checking it
against the generator's output before shipping.

THE DOSSIER SWEEP -- IT IS SYSTEMIC
Three dossiers in a row had turned out to assert things that are no longer true, so rather than
keep discovering it one element at a time, tools/dossier_sweep.py now audits all 47 against the
sealed corpus. 25 of 47 cite at least one DEAD claim id. 44 of 47 understate their own claim count
-- sodium says 14 where the corpus holds 66, vitamin-b12 says 37 against 75, vitamin-e 68 against
104. 42 carry a flat "this material does not exist, do not use it" assertion, and several are now
false. The sharpest evidence: two concepts Luneth actually PICKED -- B2's "The glow that named it"
and B5's "Found by accident" -- are built entirely on material their own dossier forbids as

CORRECTION TO THE RECORD: chronicle/next-chunk.md logged boron.md as CLEAN. It is not -- it cites
the dead WAL-CLM-RARE-000098 and undercounts by 14. The old clean/dirty notes in the handoff are
not trustworthy and have been replaced by a pointer to the sweep. vitamin-b9, the element chosen
next, cites dead WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000123 and says 24 claims where the corpus holds 38.

A guard was appended to chronicle/header-research/README.md so a future session runs the sweep
before trusting a dossier at all. A dossier is a head start, never an authority.

TOOLING

B9 (folic acid) demos. Grounding started and already shapes the design: folate dominates
