summary: Folic acid (B9) header demos: seven concepts, all seven approved first time - and the element's own research dossier would have made every one of them post the government's number as Wallach's recommendation
detail:
Seven header concepts for folic acid, and Luneth approved all of them on the first round. What is worth remembering from this one is not the design. It is that the research notes for this element, written by an earlier session of me, were wrong in a way that would have put a number on the screen that Wallach spent seven books arguing against.

The notes proposed a daily target of 400 micrograms. Four days ago Luneth read the actual page of the 2014 book, we agreed it had misprinted that figure, and we deleted the claim rather than post a number he demonstrably rejects. Folate's target is 1,000 micrograms, from his own 1995 program. Had I taken the notes at face value, all seven panels would have carried the government's RDA as his recommendation. The same notes said the corpus holds 24 claims for folate when it holds 38, and stated flatly that no discovery or history material exists for this vitamin - while two of the strongest panels are built on precisely that history. This is now the third element in a row where a concept Luneth picked was built on material its own notes forbade. B2's glow, B5's yeast flask, and now B9's thirty-one-year FDA trail. The notes are a head start. They are never the authority. The sealed corpus is.

The other thing worth keeping is how the real defects were caught. The machine check came back perfect: every figure at exactly its authored size, no overlapping text, no labels running off the canvas, and the page proven to scroll by actually scrolling it. Then I looked at the screenshots and two figures were rendering a lie. The animation that fades each figure in sets opacity to full, and in CSS that instruction beats the transparency written on the shape itself - so a band meant to be a faint 13% tint came out solid orange, and two bars whose own caption called them "a paler tail" came out solid. One figure was making a false statement about its own picture, and there is no gate that can see that. A third defect was the oldest lesson in this project arriving again: a thin vertical rule I placed at what I estimated was a safe distance ran straight through every year numeral, because the display typeface is about half again as wide as my estimate. Measure, never estimate.

TECHNICAL RECORD

FILES. Seven new fragments in temporary/header-fragments/vb9-frags/ as .htmlfrag (vb9-a-before, vb9-b-half, vb9-c-locked, vb9-d-mask, vb9-e-skin, vb9-f-31years, vb9-g-scale), each written through safe_write rewrite from a UTF-8 LF payload staged in the scratchpad. Assembled from one shared style block plus one shared why-block plus a per-concept body, so a chrome fix lands in all seven at once rather than seven times. Demo: temporary/awaiting-refinement/vitamin-b9-demos-r1.html, 79,632 chars, 7 panels, built by tools/mockup_harness.py --category vitamin with no accent override (orange is the vitamin default). The seven Aug-4 files already sitting in vb9-frags as .html were left alone and deliberately not reused: every one hardcodes the overturned 400 mcg, and vb9-a-rda's whole thesis was that he printed the government's folate number beside his own, which is a concept built on the misprint itself. They were never presented to Luneth and appear in no log.

THE SEVEN CONCEPTS. A, "Six months before" - the only folate instruction in his books with a clock on it, drawn as a prevention band running from six months before conception through early pregnancy, ending at a third stop labelled "after it has formed, surgery is the only treatment", with 98% as the hero number and an in-panel flag that the 98% is his own laboratory and farm-animal work rather than a human trial (DDDL-000042, LETS-000365, LETS-000359). B, "Half the answer" - a single bar standing for spina bifida split into two labelled halves, folic acid preventing 50% and zinc the other 50%. This is the rare place where Wallach caps his own nutrient, and it is the honest answer to the overlap-dashboard constraint stated in his voice rather than derived from our claim counts (RARE-000343). C, "Locked" - two lanes: with B12, bound folate is released into free folate that can be absorbed, transported and stored; without it, the same folate stays bound and you are deficient at optimal intake (EPIGEN-000262, EPIGEN-000261). D, "The masking effect" - two tracks diverging from a marked moment where folic acid is given, the anemia climbing to marked improvement while the gut and nerves keep descending, unchecked (IMMORT-000302). E, "Three skin complaints" - psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis and vitiligo as three abstract labelled marks with his folate dose under each, plus the loop that vitiligo is also on his own folate deficiency list (LETS-000409, LETS-000430, LETS-000462, LETS-000010). F, "Thirty-one years" - 1930 yeast, 1946 isolated, a thirty-one-year restriction bar, 1996 flour fortification, 1998, with -20% as the hero; the first substantial use of Hell's Kitchen in any header (HELLS-000035, EPIGEN-000265, RARE-000239). G, "Every folate figure on one scale" - five bars to a 75,000 mcg full width of which only the second is a daily amount, hero 75x, and a ceiling quote that an overdose causes a relative zinc deficiency (LETS-000052, DDDL-000080, LETS-000267, LETS-000288, EPIGEN-000264, EPIGEN-000263).

GROUNDING. All 38 sealed claims read in full through claim_review.py --entity vitamin-b9; the slug is vitamin-b9, not folic-acid. All 22 cited ids re-verified live in a single claim_review --ids pass with zero missing. The target matches essentials-targets-data.json exactly: kind wallach, low 1000.0 mcg, source WAL-CLM-LETS-000052, provenance original_low equal to upper_taken equal to 1000.0. The why-block states the 1995 row in its true column order (400 government RDA, 1,000 his true supplement need, 15 to 20 mg short course) and carries the ratified-divergence-74 flag explaining why favour-newest does not reach for the newer book here. The misprint ruling was verified from source rather than from memory: git log -S surfaced commit 4b962ea0, "corpus: delete the misprinted 2014 folate claim, ship folate at 1,000 mcg", and claim_review confirms WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000123 is not in the sealed corpus. Note that "Folic acid 400 mcg" still appears byte-exact inside two live claims' verbatim windows, as the neighbouring row of the biotin and choline entries from the same 2014 table - context, not a folate dose claim. Book titles and editions were read from books-meta.json, the registry that is the authority, not typed from memory: Let's Play Doctor is 4th ed. 1995 and Hell's Kitchen is 3rd ed. 2015. Two verbatims were trimmed at both ends to a complete clause rather than quoted out to their sealed boundary, because RARE-000343's slice ends mid-sentence at "the other 50%" and EPIGEN-000262's contains an OCR comma in "so it, can be absorbed" - both remain byte-exact contiguous slices, and no severed thought is shown to a reader. The 98%, the six-months-before instruction and zinc's half are claim_text rather than verbatim, so they are cited and never quote-marked.

VERIFIED. mockup_measure: seven of seven figures authored at 700 and rendered at 700, scale 1.000; zero text collisions; zero clipped labels; scrolling proven by a real wheel event moving 900px through 11,752px of content. Every one of the seven panels was screenshotted at deviceScaleFactor 2 and read with my own eyes twice, before and after the fixes. temporary/build-scripts/demo_quote_gate.py passes, so all seven use the real .ds-pull-quote with .ds-mark and a footer attribution rather than the hand-rolled quote that regressed niacin, B1 and B6. Board 90/90 with zero new reds; 23 of those 90 gates bear on truth outside our own files, so green means nothing drifted, not that anything is right. build.mjs exit 0, build parity fresh.

DEFECTS FOUND BY EYE AND FIXED IN THE SAME PASS. First and most important: the rule .vb9-anim.vb9-in .vb9-rv { opacity: 1 } overrides an SVG opacity presentation attribute, so concept A's 13% tint band rendered solid orange and concept G's two paler range tails rendered solid, which made G's caption a false statement about its own figure. Every affected attribute was converted to fill-opacity or stroke-opacity, all seven bodies were grepped to prove no bare opacity attribute survives on any reveal element (the three that remain sit on a rule or on a child of a reveal group, both unaffected), and the warning now lives in the shared stylesheet so the next fragment cannot repeat it. This is the documented attribute-loses-to-CSS trap arriving from a new direction: my own reveal CSS rather than a fill. Second: concept F's vertical spine at x=90 ran through the right edge of every year numeral, four characters of display bold measuring about 48px against my 34px estimate; the spine was removed and the rows align without it. Third: concept C's "no B12" label dangled below-left of its marker and was moved directly above it. Fourth: concept E's vitiligo mark at ink-medium .78 out-weighed its two accent siblings and read as a different visual family, so it moved into the accent family at .62. Fifth: concept A's headline orphaned a bare "it." on its second line, fixed by dropping the trailing word.

PROCESS. Two already-approved sets, B2 r4 and B5 r1, were screenshotted before anything was designed, per the lesson from B2's three rejections, and the approved panel anatomy was copied one-to-one before adapting: eyebrow, kill headline, setup prose, a captioned figure whose parts are named inside the frame, the real pull-quote with its highlight, payoff prose with bold key phrases, the mono claim-id line, a mono caveat, and the disclaimer. Every figure passes the test of whether a reader could get the panel from the figure alone with the prose removed: a split bar, two lanes, two tracks, three named marks, five dated rows, five to-scale bars. One tooling note for future sessions: piping the screenshot script through head -3 killed node on SIGPIPE after four of seven files, and the truncated output read like a complete run - redirect to a log rather than truncating a pipe.

DEFERRED. Luneth's ratification of the lede and the 1,000 mcg why-block, which are shown above every panel and remain unratified, as they do for B1, B2, B3, B5, iodine, boron and potassium. Unused material worth a panel if an r2 is ever wanted: the McAllen, Texas anencephaly cluster that public health blamed on a chemical pollutant and Wallach reads as folate and zinc missing from a corn-tortilla winter diet (DDDL-000191); the drug drain as its own panel rather than a closing note in G (EPIGEN-000263); and pediatricians missing folate-deficiency anemia in his own children (LETS-000507). Also still true and not fixed by this round: vitamin-b9.md is wrong on disk, with a dead id, a 24-against-38 undercount and a false claim that no discovery material exists, and it belongs to the systemic dossier-drift thread already open in next-chunk.md.

summary: Vanadium header demos approved, with one concept replaced: Luneth said the colour idea was underplayed, so the weakest panel became four tubes of the element actually in solution - and the blue one turns out to be the form sold on supplement labels
detail:
Seven header concepts for vanadium. Luneth approved the set, with one instruction: the colour aspect was underplayed, concept D was the weakest by far, and it should be replaced by another colour illustration that goes further than simple colours and demonstrates the thing in realistic terms.

The replacement is worth recording because of where it landed. Vanadium's colours are not a decorative fact about it - they track how many electrons the atom has given up. So rather than coloured squares, the figure is four tubes of the same element actually in solution: glassware with a rim, empty glass above the liquid line, a curved surface, a highlight down one side, depth in the liquid, and coloured light pooling on the surface under each tube where it has passed through. Violet, green, blue, yellow, one element.

Then it stopped being a chemistry illustration and became an argument. The blue tube is vanadium in its fourth state - vanadyl - and vanadyl is exactly the form Wallach names when he says the gut takes up between a thousandth and a hundredth of what you swallow. So the panel ends on the prettiest state on the shelf being the one that mostly goes straight through you. That kept the single best fact from the discarded panel, the absorption spread, without the bar chart he had just rejected.

The honesty line on that panel needed care and is drawn twice, once in the figure's own footer and once in the caveat box. Which colour belongs to which oxidation state is general chemistry, offered as reference, because Wallach never names an individual compound - all he says is that vanadium's compounds are many and beautifully coloured, which is why the element carries a goddess's name. The absorption percentages and the daily target beside it are his. Two different kinds of fact on one panel, labelled apart rather than blended.

Also worth keeping from this round: three separate times the machine check came back perfectly clean and the screenshot showed something broken. Two labels in the first panel sat on one line and read as a single run-on sentence. Two heartbeat traces meant to show a stronger contraction were drawn on top of each other, so the entire point was invisible - it looked like one wobbly line with a shadow. And the new panel's small chip label was six pixels wider than the box it sat in, so its first and last letters were clipped by its own border. Nothing overlapped, nothing ran off the canvas, so nothing could be flagged. Eyes remain the only instrument for this.

TECHNICAL RECORD

FILES. Seven new fragments in temporary/header-fragments/van-frags/ as .htmlfrag (van-a-insulin, van-b-notgenetic, van-c-craving, van-d-colours, van-e-goddess, van-f-beyond, van-g-dogfood), each written through safe_write rewrite. The shared-chrome assembler built for B9 was derived across by sed rather than rewritten, so the two packs cannot drift apart. Demo: temporary/awaiting-refinement/vanadium-demos-r1.html, 84,650 chars, 7 panels, mockup_harness --category mineral (blue). The discarded absorption-bar panel survives as van-d-form.htmlfrag on disk but is not in the assembled page, and its scratchpad source was renamed out of the assembler's glob so it cannot be resurrected by accident.

THE SEVEN CONCEPTS. A, "It acts like insulin" - a labelled flow showing vanadium altering cell-membrane ion transport so the insulin receptor becomes more sensitive, over what was actually measured in diabetic animals fed vanadium: blood glucose the same as normal controls while serum insulin stayed low. Its quote is the 1985 University of Vancouver statement that vanadium will replace insulin for adult onset diabetics, presented in the panel as a statement he reports rather than his own prediction (DDDL-000047, DDDL-000034, DDDL-000035, DDDL-000222). B, "Not genetic" - the phrase "a genetically-transmitted disease" struck through and replaced by "a simple mineral deficiency", over the row from his own table of degenerative disease causes naming chromium, vanadium and zinc (EPIGEN-000308 byte-exact, including his exclamation mark). C, "The craving is the sign" - two labelled vessels, the soft drink marked FIRST and the water marked LAST, over the carbohydrates he names by name, with the self-feeding loop in the payoff: glucose stored as fat rather than burned, and refined sugar increasing urinary loss of the mineral by up to 300% (RARE-000039, HELLS-000055, LETS-000508). D, "Four colours in a glass" - the replacement described above (RARE-000253, DDDL-000224, IMMORT-000345, EPIGEN-000138). E, "Named for a goddess" - 1801, Andres Manuel del Rio, named for Vanadis, 0.02% of the earth's crust, over the century-and-a-half gap to 1971 essentiality and his charge that these soil elements were held to be totally toxic (IMMORT-000345, RARE-000358, RARE-000359). F, "Beyond blood sugar" - three labelled marks for the heart's inotropic effect, cholesterol synthesis inhibited in blood and aorta, and mammary tumour induction blocked in mice (RARE-000255, RARE-000256, EPIGEN-000307, DDDL-000036). G, "A dog's life" - three counted tallies, 40 minerals in Science Diet dog food, 28 in Purina rat pellets, no more than 12 in any human infant formula, with chromium, vanadium and lithium flagged totally absent (RARE-000043, RARE-000042, DDDL-000008).

GROUNDING. All 66 sealed claims read in full through claim_review.py --entity vanadium; all 28 cited ids re-verified live in one pass with zero missing. The target is the first two-step derivation on the board and the why-block states both steps rather than presenting the result as a figure lifted off a page: Epigenetics gives vanadium 50 to 100 mcg per 100 lb of body weight, the canon takes the upper end and scales that per-100-lb rule to the app's 154 lb reference, times 1.54, rounded to two significant figures, giving 150 mcg. Those numbers were read off essentials-targets-data.json's own provenance block rather than recomputed from memory. The 1995 Let's Play Doctor figure of 500 mcg survives as a corroborating claim, not the target, because the newest book wins. The why-block also carries his insulin-shock instruction - start at 25 mcg three times a day if you already take insulin - which felt indefensible to omit from a page about a mineral he says can replace insulin. Colour-by-oxidation-state is labelled as reference under supply-reference-only-when-Wallach-silent; the precedent is the USDA foods table on the potassium panel.

VERIFIED. mockup_measure: seven of seven figures authored at 700 and rendered at 700, scale 1.000; zero text collisions; zero clipped labels; scrolling proven by a real wheel event moving 900px through 12,169px of content. Every panel screenshotted at deviceScaleFactor 2 and read by eye across three rounds - the initial build, after the first fix pass, and after the D replacement. demo_quote_gate.py passes, so all seven use the real pull-quote component. Board 90/90 counted explicitly rather than asserted: 90 OK lines and 0 FAIL lines. build.mjs exit 0.

DEFECTS FOUND BY EYE AND FIXED. One, panel A's two mono sub-labels shared a baseline and read as one run-on sentence, "alters cell-membrane becomes more sensitive to insulin"; separated onto their own baselines, figure height 322 to 350. Two, panel F's two heartbeat traces were overlaid and nearly coincident so the stronger contraction was invisible; rebuilt as two beats side by side with a two-line legend naming each, height 300 to 318. Three, panel D's caption described the first bar as "5 pixels wide", which is my vocabulary and not a reader's; reworded. Four, the replacement panel's "vanadyl - the label form" chip measured 173.9px inside a 168px box and had both end glyphs clipped by its own border; box widened to 240px with 33px of padding each side, measured not estimated. Five, the black shadow discs under the tubes read as stands rather than shadows and were replaced with two-ellipse coloured light pools in each tube's own colour, which is simultaneously the more realistic choice and more colour, the thing he asked for. Six, a stray duplicated path segment in the first tube's liquid.

NEW INSTRUMENT, SCRATCHPAD ONLY, NOT WIRED INTO ANY GATE. A padding probe that pairs each SVG label with the box it sits inside and reports the clearance, written because mockup_measure compares text against text and against the viewBox edge but never against a decorative shape a label is meant to fit within - precisely the blind spot that let the vanadyl chip ship clipped. It was negative-controlled in both directions before being believed: it passes all seven boxed labels on the fixed build and fires with exit code 1 on a deliberately re-narrowed 168px box. Its own first run was wrong and said so loudly - it paired every chip in a row against every label in that row and reported ten phantom overflows with negative padding, until containment was required on both axes rather than just vertically. A probe whose first output is a false alarm is the argument for negative controls, not against them. It stays in the scratchpad deliberately: folding it into mockup_measure would change a shared tool that other packs depend on, and that was not part of this chunk.

DEFERRED. Luneth's ratification of the lede and the 150 mcg why-block. Flagged to him as his decision rather than settled by me: panels D and E now both work the colour theme, since E's abstract swatch row was a placeholder for the idea D now demonstrates properly - if both ship, E's swatches are redundant, while E's history stands on its own. Unused material if an r2 is ever wanted: the vanadium deficiency roster of fifteen clinical diseases including narcolepsy and Tourette's (DDDL-000226), the hair-analysis pattern for diabetes (RARE-000081), and the tranquilliser and antidepressant mineral-replacement tables (RARE-000276, 277, 278, 280, 282). Not repaired by this round: vanadium.md still undercounts itself by 29 on disk, part of the systemic dossier-drift thread already open in next-chunk.md.

summary: Sodium header demos banked - the element where you can quote Wallach into either position, so the honest panel prints both of his lists side by side. Luneth: good enough, needs refinement, unspecified.
detail:
Seven header concepts for sodium. Luneth's verdict was "good enough, but needs some refinement", and he closed the session there, so this is banked as a starting point and not approved as finished. He did not say what needs refining and I have deliberately not guessed. The next session must ask him before touching it.

The work that mattered on this element happened before any markup existed. Sodium is where Wallach stands furthest from mainstream medicine, and the trap is that you can quote him into either position and both quotes are real. His 2015 book says salt does not cause high blood pressure and that restricting it will shorten your life. His own 1995 sodium toxicity table lists hypertension, edema, congestive heart failure and renal failure. A panel built on either sentence alone would misrepresent him.

So one panel prints both lists side by side, unedited, and states inside the figure that the same author wrote them nineteen years apart. He does reconcile them, but only by moving the cause: he argues the salt sensitivity seen in high blood pressure comes from restricted calcium and potassium rather than from the salt. That reconciliation sits in the closing paragraph rather than being smuggled up into the headline, and every panel touching blood pressure or salt restriction carries a note saying plainly that this contradicts consensus and is not advice. Someone on a prescribed low-sodium diet for heart failure could land on this page, and the page should not read as permission.

The other thing worth keeping is that I walked into a trap I had documented myself one element earlier. The salt block's ground shadow carried a plain opacity attribute on an element that the reveal animation forces to full opacity, so it rendered as a solid black oval - the identical defect I had fixed on the vanadium tubes, with my own warning about it sitting in the stylesheet I had just copied across. Knowing a trap and writing it down is not the same as not falling into it. This time I stopped looking with my eyes and wrote a scan that parses every SVG tag for the combination; it found exactly one, matching what the screenshot showed.

TECHNICAL RECORD

FILES. Seven new fragments in temporary/header-fragments/na-frags/ (na-a-metalgas, na-b-saltblock, na-c-fortyeight, na-d-heatwave, na-e-stomachacid, na-f-bothlists, na-g-worthsalt), written through safe_write. The directory had to be created first: safe_write does not create parent directories, and its failure surfaces as a bare FileNotFoundError on the temporary .tmp path, which reads like a permissions problem and is not one. Demo: temporary/awaiting-refinement/sodium-demos-r1.html, 87,013 chars, 7 panels, category mineral. Chrome derived from the vanadium pack by sed, plus two new figure classes for a plus glyph and an in-figure hero number.

THE SEVEN CONCEPTS. A, what salt is actually made of - realistic: a lump of sodium metal in a jar of oil, a flask of yellow-green chlorine, and salt drawn as isometric cubes, over the National Geographic passage he quotes to open his minerals chapter about a metal that bursts into flame in water and a lethal gas being an absolute necessity for life (RARE-000378, IMMORT-000372, IMMORT-000377, IMMORT-000375, RARE-000187). B, the salt block - realistic: a weathered block hollowed where animals have licked it, labelled with the 85 percent minimum below which animals ignore it even when badly deficient, plus the 0.5 percent of diet they eat as salt and his claim that they never develop high blood pressure or stroke, under the line about the medical profession thinking humans are dumber than cows (HELLS-000065, EPIGEN-000330, IMMORT-000374, RARE-000026). C, forty-eight hours - the 1940 Richter case as a four-stop timeline: licking salt off crackers at one year, eating it from the shaker at eighteen months, hospitalised at three and a half to restrict it, dead forty-eight hours later, autopsy showing Addison's disease (EPIGEN-000331, DDDL-000242, IMMORT-000314). D, the heat wave of 1993 - two labelled columns, seventy to a hundred grams of salt a day lost in sweat against the 0.9 percent saline that treated the survivors, over what he says the dead had in common (DDDL-000244, EPIGEN-000320, RARE-000027, RARE-000190). E, your stomach acid is made out of salt - sodium chloride to hydrochloric acid, fanning out to protein digestion via pepsin, B12 via intrinsic factor, and mineral absorption, with hypochlorhydria named as the failure state (HELLS-000059, DDDL-000261, DDDL-000265, EPIGEN-000323, EPIGEN-000325). F, both of these are his - the honesty panel described above (HELLS-000061, LETS-000033, EPIGEN-000332, RARE-000367, EPIGEN-000328). G, worth their salt - salarium behind the word salary, the Via Salacia, cattle blood and urine drunk in salt-poor Africa, and everything owned given for salt on the Sierra Leone coast (EPIGEN-000333, EPIGEN-000334, EPIGEN-000322, RARE-000369).

GROUNDING. All 66 sealed claims read in full; the dossier claims 14, the worst undercount in the whole set, and it was not used for design. Target 3,300 mg from LETS-000066, matching the canon exactly. The why-block is unusually well corroborated and says so: the 1995 base-line row gives 3,300 mg of sodium, and the 2014 book gives the requirement as six to ten grams of salt a day, or half a percent of the dry weight of the diet. Salt is 39.34 percent sodium by weight, computed rather than recalled, so six to ten grams of salt is 2,360 to 3,933 mg of sodium and the 3,300 mg target sits inside it, working out at about 8.4 grams of salt a day. Two books nineteen years apart agreeing once the units are reconciled is worth more than either figure alone. The conversion is flagged in the panel as ours rather than his, because he states one figure as salt and the other as sodium. One oddity is left on the record rather than smoothed away: the 300 to 3,000 mg thirty-day figure on that 1995 row is lower than his own daily target, the reverse of every other row in the table.

VERIFIED. Seven of seven figures at scale 1.000, zero text collisions, zero clipped labels, scrolling proven by a real wheel event through 12,331px of content. The boxed-label padding probe reports four of four clear. Every panel screenshotted at double scale and read by eye twice. Board 90/90 counted explicitly, ninety OK lines and zero failures. Build exit 0.

DEFECTS FOUND AND FIXED. The clipped-label check earned its keep twice: one caption ran 97.1px off its own viewBox and another 71.8px, both because I estimated the caption face at about six pixels per character when it renders at about seven. Both split onto two lines with the figures grown to match. The reveal-opacity defect described above. And the salt crystals, first drawn as diamonds that read as abstract gems, redrawn as isometric cubes, which is what salt actually forms.

DEFERRED AND OPEN. Sodium needs unspecified refinement - ask, do not guess. The lede and the 3,300 mg why-block are unratified. A finding worth acting on separately: LETS-000032, his twenty-two-sign sodium deficiency roster, has no authored question and no short answer in the enrichment store, making it the only claim in this pack that Ask Wallach cannot answer from - and "what are the symptoms of low sodium" is the most obvious question anyone would type. Unused material: the Japanese comparison, where the newer book says fifteen grams a day with eighty-five percent less cardiovascular disease while the older says twenty-eight, so favour-newest picks fifteen and the two must never appear side by side as books disagreeing; the 1997 Sodium Task Force six-hundred-percent heart-attack figure; pregnancy toxemia and the pregnancy salt requirement; water intoxication in infants fed low-sodium formula; and potassium-deficient rats licking everything in sight.

summary: Session close: three elements taken from nothing to banked demo sets - folic acid, vanadium and sodium - and the standing lesson is that a green measurement board sat alongside a broken picture in every single round.
detail:
Three elements went from nothing to banked demo sets this session: folic acid, vanadium and sodium. Twenty-one concepts, all screenshotted and read rather than assumed. Folic acid and vanadium are approved; sodium is banked and needs refinement Luneth has not yet specified.

The thread running through all three is worth stating on its own, because it did not vary once. In every round the machine checks came back clean - every figure at its true authored size, no overlapping text, no labels off the canvas, the page proven to scroll by actually scrolling it - and in every round the screenshot then showed something broken. A band meant to be a faint tint rendered solid orange. Two heartbeat traces meant to show a stronger contraction were drawn on top of each other, so the whole point was invisible. Two labels shared a line and read as one run-on sentence. A chip label was six pixels wider than the box it sat in and had its first and last letters clipped by its own border. A shadow rendered as a solid black oval. Not one of those is visible to a probe that compares text against text, and every one of them was obvious within a second of looking at the picture.

The second thread is that the research dossiers were wrong on every element I touched. Folic acid's proposed a daily target of 400 micrograms, which is the exact number we had thrown out four days earlier as a misprint in the book, and would have posted the government's figure as Wallach's recommendation on all seven panels. Vanadium's undercounted itself by twenty-nine claims. Sodium's says fourteen claims against an actual sixty-six, the worst in the set. In all three cases the correct move was the same: read every sealed claim, verify the target against the canon's own provenance and the commit history rather than a dossier, and design from that.

The third is a piece of Luneth's taste, learned the hard way on vanadium. Told that the colour aspect was underplayed and that a panel was the weakest by far, the wrong response is a richer palette. The right one is a realistic demonstration that carries an argument - four tubes of the element actually in solution, where the blue one turns out to be the form sold on supplement labels and absorbed at a hundredth of the dose. Demonstrate, do not decorate.

Handoff is set for a fresh genesis start. Board 90/90 with zero new reds, build parity fresh, the Creator's Log a pure append at 829 entries, and everything committed and pushed.

summary: Manganese header demos: two rounds built, both rejected. What survives is the answer to the question he actually asked -- why an extra manganese saved a dying man when the 90-essential programme alone did not.
detail:
Luneth asked for manganese header concepts and I built them twice. He turned down both. The
first round he called illustrations that "mean nothing, illustrate nothing, teach nothing, reveal
nothing at a glance" and asked for a complete re-do where every figure serves a purpose. The second
round -- where I rebuilt every figure to teach -- came back "worse across the board than the first."
He gave no reason either time, so no reason is recorded here as his.

In between, he asked something better than a design question. A Wallach-based doctor had pulled his
grandfather back from death's door on the 90-essential programme plus one extra manganese in liquid
form, and he wanted to know the mechanism: why that mineral, and why the programme alone was not
enough. That question got answered, it is sourced, and it outlives the demos.

MY DIAGNOSIS OF THE SECOND FAILURE -- a diagnosis, not his words. Told the figures taught nothing, I
made all six teach and in doing so turned them into charts, diagrams and cross-sections. That is the
exact idiom this project has already rejected twice, both times recorded in the handoff I was reading
from: B6 round one ("clearly lower quality than the rest ... it's the way it's presented", diagnosed
then as a drift to infographic idioms instead of singular hero images) and chromium (a boxed loop, a
bar chart, a stat dashboard reads "boring/clinical"). I fixed the stated fault by walking into a
documented one. The two demands are not in tension and the next round has to meet both: a figure must
teach at a glance AND be a hero image rather than a chart. The approved sets already do both -- the
niacin furnace teaches convergence and is a hero, the B1 rice grain teaches polishing and is a hero,
the vanadium tubes teach oxidation state and are beautiful.

THE MECHANISM, in his own sources -- three reasons an extra manganese is not a deviation from Wallach's
programme but a step his own text prescribes:

1. He says the colloidal base needs a manganese top-up himself. Dead Doctors Don't Lie, describing the
   Toddy colloidal minerals his whole programme is built on: "The colloidal minerals were all present
   in trace amounts. They required an additional source of the major minerals and electrolytes such as
   calcium, magnesium, manganese, zinc, and potassium to even come close to the published RDAs."
   Manganese is one of only five minerals he names. NOT YET A SEALED CLAIM.

2. The daily programme delivers a maintenance dose; his own table carries a corrective column up to
   5.5 times larger. Base Line Fig. 8-1, manganese row: RDA 2.5 mg / True Supplement Need 5 mg /
   30-Day Pharmacologic 2 to 50 mg (LETS-000057). Of that third column he writes that it is "used in
   extraordinary situations when your body requires large amounts of raw material to restore and
   replenish overworked organs and tissues" -- NOT YET SEALED. His own manganese prescriptions sit in
   that upper band: 10-15 mg/day for tardive dyskinesia (LETS-000445), 50 mg/day for epilepsy
   (LETS-000267, DDDL-000236).

3. A failing body absorbs badly, so the form is the point -- which is why it was a liquid. "YOU ARE NOT
   WHAT YOU EAT-YOU ARE WHAT YOU ABSORB!" (Epigenetics, his capitals, NOT YET SEALED), over an
   absorption ladder that IS sealed: metallic forms 1-10% (IMMORT-000291, IMMORT-000292, RARE-000106),
   chelated 25-50%, plant-derived colloidal up to 98% (DDDL-000051, LETS-000146, LETS-000197). And he
   prescribes manganese in that exact form by name -- "plant derived colloidal arsenic, manganese, and
   choline" (DDDL-000235, DDDL-000219), and "colloidal mineral suspensions that contain magnesium and
   manganese" for asthma, which he defines outright as a disease of malabsorption (LETS-000147,
   DDDL-000053). His liquid dose: one ounce per 100 pounds of body weight per day.

WHAT THE NUMBERS ACTUALLY SAY, so the story is never told wrong. I checked the stack against the sealed
product database rather than assuming it fell short. Ultimate Classic 5.0 mg + Ultimate Daily 2.0 mg +
Ultimate Gluco-Gel 2.0 mg = 9.00 mg of manganese against a 7.7 mg daily target. It CLEARS the target.
Beyond Tangy Tangerine, Ultimate EFA Plus, Ultimate Enzymes and Osteo FX carry no manganese at all. So
"the programme was not enough" is NOT a daily-target shortfall and must never be presented as one -- the
real gap is maintenance versus corrective. Composition only, per the prime directive: what a product
contains is never a Wallach recommendation. As for which liquid it was, I cannot identify it and did not
pretend to; the one candidate that fits is Ultra Body Toddy at 5.0 mg, the only other top-tier liquid in
the line and the descendant of the "Toddy" colloidal base Wallach names -- flagged as inference.

A CORRECTION I OWED HIM, logged in the chunk that found it. The manganese dossier flags RARE-000177 as
having a claim_text that outruns its verbatim on the "100,000 carpal-tunnel operations at $4,000 each"
and "over $29,000 per case" figures, and I repeated that to him as fact. Reading the actual book pages,
those figures are printed -- in both Rare Earths: Forbidden Cures and Dead Doctors Don't Lie. The
claim_text is correct and the sealed verbatim is trimmed too short. The dossier also cites RARE-000174
and RARE-000176, neither of which is in the sealed corpus any more. Both corrections are written into
next-chunk.md so the next session cannot inherit them as true.

Manganese now sits beside sodium as an element carrying an ask whose reason he did not state. The
handoff says the same thing about both: ask him, do not guess, do not rebuild, do not improve it.

summary: Three manganese rounds rejected in a row, and Luneth called it: rules I had written were forcing every illustration into the same shape. Cleared them, rebuilt from the 33 references he picked, and both manganese and cobalt landed.
detail:
Three rounds of manganese header demos were rejected one after another. The third got the
sharpest verdict yet -- "Every single illustration is both unbelievably corny, and almost completely
pointless. You're not illustrating anything, you're just making ugly svg images" -- and then Luneth
did something more useful than describe what he disliked. He named a cause: "you must have written
restrictive rules AGAIN that need to be cleared."

He was right, and the cause turned out to be documentation rather than taste. Two files were doing it.
The session handoff told the next session to "copy the panel anatomy 1:1" off the last approved
header. A memory file that loads on every single turn had taken one fix for one old rejection --
label the parts of a figure -- and promoted it into "THE RULE THAT SUBSUMES ALL". Follow both exactly
and you get flat static SVGs of literal props: a quill drawn for "1717", a tap for "tap water", an
inhaler for "asthma". Drawing the noun in the headline is the corniness. Meanwhile the guidance that
would have freed the work -- the element-headers skill, which says animation and canvas and real
imagery are all encouraged, and the 33 CodePen references Luneth hand-picked with his own notes on
each -- only loads when something happens to match it. Always-loaded beats on-demand, every time.
That is the third time this exact mechanism has caused a regression: Vitamin D, then B6, then
manganese.

So the fix was to clear the rules rather than try harder inside them, and then to actually open the
folder of references. Reading his notes rather than the titles is what changed the work. His note on
the liquid thermometer says "the move-able slider effect WITHIN THE THERMOMETER ITSELF is so unique"
-- that sentence is why manganese's dose ladder has its handle inside the tube instead of a slider
bolted alongside. His note on the highlight-marks pen says it "could for highlighting parts of
Wallach quotes that are important" -- so one manganese panel is a mark that sweeps down his own
deficiency list and stops on the three entries about fertility. His note on the brownian organism
says "I LOVE how alive and random this looks, it looks like a living organism trying to get out not
some loop", and the capture file spells out the mechanism: re-randomise velocity every frame so there
is no period at all. That is what drives the particles at the gut wall, and the bacteria assembling a
B12 molecule around a cobalt atom.

Manganese r4 was approved at four concepts. Cobalt r1 was approved in part and corrected in a way
worth recording: "Both A and D would be better if the user could control the timeline/slider instead
of autoplaying on a loop. B and C are weak, and go back to doing 6 demos again, I felt like that was
working better." Cobalt r2 is six concepts with every control in the reader's hands, and the ambient
motion left running when a figure is parked so it does not look dead.

The other lesson is about verification. An interactive figure lies far more convincingly than a
static one, because it moves and movement reads as function. Four defects this session would have
survived any screenshot. Cobalt's metal selector never had its JavaScript passed to the assembler at
all -- it rendered beautifully and did nothing; the sweep hit "not a function" on the first call.
Manganese's absorption animation measured MORE absorbed particles at his 1-10% form than at his
25-50% form, exactly backwards, because switching forms left the previous form's particles stranded
on the far side. Manganese's first dose control used a rotated native range input, which cannot align
its thumb to a non-linear scale, so the handle sat at 50 mg while the readout said 7.7. And a range
thumb travels inside the track minus its own width, so a marker positioned at the same percentage
drifts from it. None of that is visible by looking once. All of it is visible by sweeping every state
and counting pixels.

One correction against myself, logged here so it cannot be inherited: while checking the cobalt
dossier for dead claim ids, an ad-hoc probe I wrote globbed a directory that does not exist and
reported all thirteen ids dead. I had read most of those same ids as live minutes earlier. Claims
live in eden/corpus/claims/*.json under the key "id", not "claim_id", and the true answer is two dead
ids. A probe's first output is not evidence -- negative-control it before reporting from it.

Cobalt also turned out to be structurally unique on this board: it is the only essential whose card
carries no number of its own. It mirrors vitamin B12, because Wallach's position is that there is no
free-standing cobalt requirement to state. His words: "a pure cobalt requirement is only found in
some bacteria and algae." That is not a gap in the data. It is the most interesting thing about the
element, and it became the header thesis -- you do not have a cobalt requirement, you have a
requirement for what a microbe makes out of cobalt.

Nothing shipped live. Both packs sit in temporary/awaiting-refinement/ awaiting his picks, which is
where every header stays until he says otherwise.

summary: Phosphorus headers approved on the second try - and the first round's two failures turned out to be mechanical, not matters of taste, so both are now written down.
detail:
Phosphorus is the odd one out among the ninety: it is the only nutrient whose recommended
amount is zero. Wallach says you already get far too much of it, and that the surplus quietly drags
calcium out of your bones. So this card's whole job is to explain a number that looks, at first
glance, like missing data.

The first six designs were rejected outright. Two of them were called childish clip-art and the
other four read as walls of text. What makes this worth logging is that neither problem was really
about taste - each had a specific, findable cause, and both had bitten before:

The walls of text happened because the headline style used by every previous header is locked to a
small size by a rule elsewhere in the stylesheet. Written that way, a headline comes out at roughly
the size of body text, so a panel reads like a document no matter how good the writing is. Larger
sizes were available the whole time and had gone unused across four rounds. The fix was to stop
borrowing that style and write a new one.

The clip-art happened because two panels drew a picture of the thing their own headline already
named - broccoli under a headline about broccoli. That teaches the reader nothing they had not just
read, and at this size a hand-drawn object always looks cheap. The reference material Luneth
collected contains no pictures of objects at all; it is entirely typography and abstract light. The
replacement panel takes the story of how phosphorus got its name - it was boiled out of urine in
1669 and glowed in the dark - and instead of drawing a glowing lump, it makes the word PHOSPHORUS
itself give off light as you drag the room dark. Nothing is drawn.

Two smaller lessons about trusting instruments. A label collision of eighteen pixels sat in the
first round while the automated check reported no collisions and my own estimate said it cleared;
only measuring the actual positions found it. And in the second round my own overflow check raised a
false alarm on a glow layer that is deliberately wider than its frame but invisibly trimmed by it -
so the check now tests what is actually painted rather than what the box measures.

Separately, the research file for phosphorus was wrong by roughly a factor of three - it described
thirteen source passages where the sealed corpus holds thirty-four, and three of its warnings about
what could not be quoted were false. It had missed the best material in the element, including the
food table and the naming story. Corrected in place.

summary: Germanium headers approved first time - and the one thing that went wrong was a simulation that looked convincing and proved nothing, which took three tries to measure.
detail:
Germanium has the best origin story of any of the ninety. It existed on paper before anyone
had ever seen it: Mendeleyev left an empty square in the periodic table in 1871, described roughly
what belonged there, and fifteen years later a German chemist isolated exactly that and named it
germanium. The table was ordered well enough that a missing entry was itself information.

This pack was approved on the first round, which has not happened for a while. The reason is worth
recording: it was built to the standard the rejected phosphorus round forced us to write down - a
headline style that is not locked to body-text size, and no panel that draws a picture of the thing
its own headline already names. Nothing in the six panels is an illustration of an object.

The one real problem was in the panel I liked most. Germanium is a semiconductor: it takes an
electron and passes it on, and adding a trace of another element - "doping" - makes it conduct far
better. Wallach says the same electron-passing behaviour is what it does inside your cells. So the
panel is a field of electrons moving through a lattice, with a slider for doping and a switch that
relabels the identical motion from "in a transistor" to "in a cell".

It looked right and it was doing nothing. Dragging the doping made more electrons appear, but it
also made them travel faster, so they left the far side just as much sooner - and the number on
screen at any moment barely changed. A still image of it would have passed any review. The fix was
to make doping increase how many electrons there are and leave their speed almost alone, which is
also the more honest physics.

Then the measuring instrument turned out to be wrong twice, and both times the right fix was in the
instrument rather than in the standard it was checking against. First, counting bright pixels
under-reports the effect badly, because once electrons are close together their glows overlap and
stop adding up - it reported a twelvefold change as twofold. So the check now reads the number the
simulation itself is tracking, as well as what reaches the screen. Second, electrons appear at
random, so a single instantaneous reading is just luck; two settings that genuinely differed
measured almost the same. It now averages six readings at each setting. Neither fix involved
lowering the bar.

summary: Wallach's sourcing ladder verified against all 7 books before it ships as doctrine - it holds, but "colloidal" on a label does NOT mean the good kind, and a scanning typo had one chromium number 10x too big.
detail:
Before telling anyone "buy this form, avoid that one," we had to check that the rule was actually Wallach's. It wasn't verified - it came from a design mockup. So I read every mention of mineral form and absorption across all seven books.

The ladder holds. His numbers: ordinary metallic minerals (the carbonate/oxide/gluconate forms in most tablets) absorb at 8-12%, and only 3-5% once you're past 35-40. Chelated forms reach 40-65%. Plant-derived colloidal reaches 98%.

The important discovery is the one the mockup missed: "colloidal" on a label does not mean you're getting the good kind. Wallach sorts colloidal supplements into four types, and type 1 - bare "rock flour" from clay, sea beds and glacial milk - is in his own words "in fact a metallic mineral." Products are sold as colloidal today that are exactly that. Only the type made by living plants carries the 98%. He proves it on the Hunza: they absorb barely any of the mineral water they drink, and their longevity comes from IRRIGATING with it so the plants do the conversion.

I also found and fixed a scanning error. Immortality said 50-100 micrograms of food chromium yields "0.25 to 5" micrograms usable. Two other books carry that identical sentence with 0.25 to 0.5 - a dropped "0." made the number ten times too big.

Luneth ruled four cross-book conflicts. The most instructive: chelated minerals were invented in the 1960s, not the 1940s, even though the two NEWEST books say 1940s. Our favour-the-newest-book rule would have picked the wrong answer. That rule only breaks ties between defensible readings - where outside knowledge shows one side is simply wrong, recency is irrelevant.

He also caught me manufacturing a contradiction that didn't exist. I read "no less than 60 minerals" against "no less than seventy seven" as a revision needing a ruling. Both are FLOORS - 77 satisfies "no less than 60." Inventing a conflict wastes his time worse than missing one.

TECHNICAL RECORD

Ladder anchors: metallic 8-12%/3-5% IMMORT-000292, HELLS-000017, EPIGEN-000060; chelated 40-65% "a 400% increase" IMMORT-000023 (RARE-000349 = superseded flat 40%); colloidal 98% RARE-000061 p.213; four-forms taxonomy IMMORT-000026 + HK pp.219-220; Hunza "five to 12 per cent" RARE-000072; vehicle dose 1 fl oz/100 lb/day EPIGEN-000089. Per-element ladders for vanadium, chromium, phosphorus, magnesium, calcium, iron, cobalt, iodine, lithium, germanium, arsenic. summary: Fixed the scanner hanging on “Reading the label…” forever when a label image is uploaded and pasted at the same time. The newest image now wins; the older read is dropped. Root cause: two OCR runs double-loaded the engine and wedged the worker so it never returned.
detail:
When you uploaded a label image and pasted one at the same time, the scanner froze on “Reading the label…” forever. Two scans started at once, both loaded the OCR engine, and re-loading it mid-run jammed the worker so it never returned an answer. Now a newer image simply replaces an older one that is still being read, and any read that fails cleanly resets instead of hanging.

ROOT CAUSE (reproduced on the real file:// app with puppeteer):
- No re-entrancy guard: an upload + a paste fired together each ran a full OCR pipeline (repro: workersCreated=2).
- loadTesseract() early-returned only if window.Tesseract was already defined; on a fresh scanner both concurrent scans saw it undefined and each appended <script src=…/tesseract.min.js> (repro: 2 script tags). Re-running the UMD clobbers the first worker’s module state mid-init, so worker.recognize() never settles → state stays 'scanning' → “Reading the label…” forever, PAGE_ERRORS=0 (a silent never-settle, not a thrown error).
- FileReader had a 'load' handler only; an 'error'/'abort' left the same permanent 'scanning'.

FIX:
- state/ocr.ts: loadTesseract() now caches a module-level in-flight Promise (tesseractLoad); concurrent callers share ONE injection; reset to null on script error so a later scan can retry.
- views/scanner.ts: LAST-WINS. A monotonic scanSeq is bumped on every handleImageFile(); the previous reader is aborted; the load handler and the ocrToLabel().then both no-op when seq !== scanSeq, so a superseded scan’s late result can never clobber the current view. failScan(seq, e) is seq-guarded and also handles the reader 'error'/'abort'. imageDataUrl reset at scan start.

BEHAVIOUR (Luneth’s call): LAST-WINS — the newest image supersedes any in-flight scan (chosen over first-wins / ignore-the-second).

summary: The scanner now reads labels when you just open dashboard.html — no launcher, flag, or server. A live progress bar exposed the real bug (file:// blocks fetching the OCR model); fixed by bundling the model into a self-contained worker. Plus fail-loud error cards.
detail:
After the last-wins fix, the scanner STILL hung the first time you scanned — and you were right that a progress bar would expose why. It did: the bar froze at “Load engine”, which pointed straight at the cause. When the app is opened as a plain file (file://), the browser refuses to let the page fetch() its own local language-model file, so the OCR engine never got its model and hung forever. The fix bundles that model directly into the OCR worker, so nothing needs fetching — OCR now works just by opening dashboard.html. Over http (your future online version) it uses the normal lighter path with no bundled bloat. It also fails loudly now: a clear error card with a Try-again button instead of an endless spinner.

ROOT CAUSE (reproduced on the real file:// app): the vendored Tesseract worker loads eng.traineddata.gz via (env==='webworker'?fetch:...)(_) — the global fetch. On file:// the browser blocks fetch() of local files (net::ERR_FAILED, 'Failed to fetch'), an uncaught rejection that never settles createWorker, so the Scan step hung on 'Loading the language model'. Everything else loads fine because it uses importScripts (allowed on file://). Confirmed the fix direction two ways: --allow-file-access-from-files made it work (0.5s), and http worked natively — both prove fetch was the blocker.

THE FIX — bundle the model, no fetch:
- dashboard/assets/vendor/tesseract/worker-offline.js: one self-contained worker = [model base64] + [a self.fetch patch that serves the bundled model to any *.traineddata request] + [the vendored worker.min.js]. Tesseract wraps the worker as new Blob(['importScripts("<abs url>")']); a blob worker CAN importScripts an absolute file:// script (that is why worker.min.js works) but a relative import resolves against the blob base — so everything lives in ONE file with no relative imports. Generated by tools/build.mjs (idempotent; regenerates from worker.min.js + eng.traineddata.gz so it can never drift). git-force-added (~16MB) because the tesseract dir is gitignored and GitHub downloads only include tracked files — the offline-download case needs it present.
- state/ocr.ts: workerPath = onFile ? worker-offline.js : worker.min.js (window.location.protocol). The reachability preflight (assertModelReachable, a headers-only fetch) runs on http ONLY — on file:// the model is bundled, no fetch. A 60s withTimeout backstops any stall. Errors surface as typed codes (OCR_MODEL_UNREACHABLE / OCR_TIMEOUT).

PROGRESS INDICATOR (concept C, screenshot-approved earlier):
- state/ocr emits ProgressUpdate {stage 0|1|2, message, determinate, fraction} via lcscan:progress.
- views/scanner.renderScanning() renders the staged pills (Prepare / Load engine / Read label) + bar + note; mount.onProgress updates them in place (no re-render). Setup phases are an indeterminate sweep; the read phase fills with Tesseract's real recognition %. Honest — no fake timings.

FAIL-LOUD:
- views/scanner: scanError state + renderScanError() card (Couldn't read the label + Try again), shown instead of an infinite spinner; cleared on a new scan. failScan maps the typed codes to plain guidance.

detail:
This session was a big user-experience pass on Dr. Wallach's health dashboard, driven by Luneth's live testing.

THE SCANNER. The biggest fix: a scanned product could never be told 'Add' — it was always capped at 'Save' — because the verdict demanded a 'chemical form' score that only exists in the Youngevity product database, never on a photographed label, so every scan scored 0. Now, when the form can't be read from a photo, the app judges the product on what a photo DOES show (does it fill gaps in your 90, clean ingredients) and shows an honest 'form not on a label' instead of a damning 0%. A Youngevity multivitamin now correctly earns 'Add'. Also fixed: a Saved scan that silently failed to add to your regimen (a rare id collision made the app re-open the wrong saved item — reproduced in a headless run, then fixed by resolving a row by its position, not its id); character limits on every input; and a re-opened Saved item now says 'Delete' and removes it from the shelf.

THE CLOSE BUTTON. There were 8+ different close/x buttons in different sizes and styles across the app. They are now one standard '.ui-close' (a round button with an X, orange on hover), applied to the scanner first.

THE REGIMEN. Rebuilt the whole 'add products / manage your stack' panel (Luneth picked the roster-first design from a mockup): type-to-search shows the top 3 products with an 'Add' button and 'covers N of 90 essentials' so a layman knows what each product is; deleting an item asks first and moves it to a restorable Trash; the misleading orange 'Scan' button became a small secondary link. A tricky bug where the stack box collapsed to nothing (whenever a re-render fired while the tab was hidden) is fixed — it also fixed the 'I'm just browsing' bug Luneth found.

summary: Built the invisible half of the recycle bin: deleting a whole save snapshots the entire save into a restorable bin (keeps 7); removed items go to a separate bin (keeps 4); a full-slots restore lets you swap one out; a dashboard update won't lose any of it. No UI yet — next batch.
detail:
This is the invisible half of the recycle bin — all the data plumbing, built and proven before any of the visible popup, so the risky part (never losing your saved regimens) is locked down first.

What it does now: when you delete a whole saved regimen, the app quietly keeps a full snapshot of it — its items and its settings — in a "deleted saves" bin that holds your 7 most recent; when you remove a single item, that goes into a separate "removed items" bin that holds your 4 most recent. Nothing expires — the oldest only drops off when a bin is full. Both bins live inside your saves document (the storage choice you made), and I wrote the upgrade so a future dashboard update reads your old data and simply adds the new bin fields — it can't wipe anything. If all 4 of your save-slots are full when you go to restore a save, the app will (once the UI lands) let you pick one to move into the bin so the restored one has a place to land. There's no button for any of this yet — that's the next batch.

TECHNICAL RECORD

Storage decision (yours): the bin lives inside rgSlots_v1, not a separate key — atomic writes, §31-consistent.

Deviation from the approved plan, flagged honestly: the plan said bump the document to version 2 with a read-transform-validate migration. I used this codebase's proven backfillP4 idiom instead — the new fields are OPTIONAL and I backfill them AFTER the document already validates as version 1. This is strictly safer against data loss: with a v2 bump, a bug in the transform could yield an invalid document and trip the auto-heal that rebuilds a blank Default (wiping the user's data); with backfill-after-validate, the document is already known-good before anything is added, so a backfill bug cannot cause a wipe. Same durability goal (survive a dashboard update), safer mechanism. The migration probe proves zero loss.

Schema (core/schemas/regimen.ts): TrashEntrySchema gains slotName (optional) — the origin save's name captured at removal, so a removed item can still show where it came from even after that save is itself deleted. New SlotTrashEntrySchema = { slot: SlotSchema, deletedAt } — a whole-slot snapshot (items, overrides, colour, goals, timestamps). SlotDocSchema gains slotTrash: z.array(SlotTrashEntrySchema).max(7).optional(). Version stays literal(1). trash keeps .max(20) as a read-tolerance; the real item cap (4) is enforced by capTrash on every write and by the one-time backfill.

State (state/regimen.ts): constants MAX_ITEM_TRASH=4, MAX_SLOT_TRASH=7. capTrash caps the item bin to 4; new capSlotTrash caps the save bin to 7 (both newest-first ring buffers). backfillRecycle runs inside loadSlotDoc after backfillP4: adds slotTrash [] if absent, caps the item bin to 4, backfills each item entry's slotName from its slotId when that save still exists — persisted without emitting, a no-op once complete. deleteSlot now snapshots the WHOLE slot into slotTrash (cap 7) instead of scattering its items into the item bin — this reconciles the #8a slot-delete confirm shipped earlier today (that had put items into the item trash). saveRgRemoved captures slotName = the active save's name. restoreDeletedItem: restores to the origin save if its slotId still resolves, else the active save; dedups by id. restoreDeletedSlot(deletedAtKey, replaceSlotId?): under MAX_SLOTS it returns the snapshot directly and activates it, reusing the original slot id when that id is free (so an orphaned removed-item's origin resolves again — the edge case Luneth raised); at MAX_SLOTS it requires replaceSlotId, snapshots that current save back into the bin, and the restored save takes its place. installBridges + the Window interface gain restoreDeletedItem/restoreDeletedSlot for probe reach.

Views (views/regimen.ts): removed the slot-delete undo path (undoDelete + the DeletedSlot capture + the confirm-do undo callback + the restoreFromTrash import) — the #8a confirm plus the recycle bin supersede it. The confirm-do branch now just calls deleteSlot and shows a toast only on refusal. showToast is kept for refusals; the unstyled .ck-undo (finding #2) now only affects those.

Gate (tools/invariants.py + test_slot_invariants.py): slot_invariants now also requires SlotDocSchema.slotTrash to carry .max(7); the negative test schema_no_max7 was added, and GOOD_SCHEMA updated so baseline_good still passes. A speculative unused `export type TrashEntry` was removed (knip no_new_dead_code flagged it).

summary: The recycle bin is now visible and usable: a button in the rail opens a popup of your deleted saves (as coloured cards) and removed items, each with Restore, and the popup refreshes live. The full-slots swap step is the next batch; its machinery is already built.
detail:
The recycle bin is now something you can actually see and use. A "Restore Deleted Slots & Items" button sits in your regimen rail (it only shows up when there's something to restore). Click it and a popup opens: your deleted saves appear as little coloured cards — each showing its coverage and how many items it held — and your removed items appear below as a list. Every one has a Restore button. Restore a save or an item and it comes right back into your regimen, and the popup updates itself immediately so you can see what's left. Deleted saves that came from a save you later deleted still show a clear note that they'll restore into your active save. The only thing not wired to a button yet: if all 4 of your save-slots are full when you restore a save, you'll get a message for now — the proper "pick one to swap out" step is the very next batch, and the machinery behind it is already built and tested.

TECHNICAL RECORD

Views (views/regimen.ts): renderRail adds .rc-trigger (a dashed full-width button styled like "Add a save", pinned under the "Scan your own item" link) shown only when binCount = (slotTrash.length + trash.length) > 0. render() now emits a .rc-host overlay host next to the toast host and, if the popup is open, calls populateRecycle() after the rebuild — a recycleOpen closure flag survives the regimen:changed re-render, so restoring something refreshes the open popup in place instead of closing it. populateRecycle builds the style-D popup imperatively (all user strings via textContent, §00.B #5): a .rc-gal gallery of the slotTrash entries as faithful mini-tiles (coveredCountForItems(entry.slot.items, entry.slot.overrides) for the NN/90, the slot's own palette hue with the same isSlotColour fallback the live .ck-slot tiles use, relAge(entry.deletedAt) for the timer, item count), then a removed-items list whose meta reads "from <slotName> · <when>" when the origin save still resolves, else "<slotName> · deleted · will restore to active save slot · <when>". openRecycle/closeRecycle toggle the flag + host. The delegated clickHandler gained branches: rc-open, rc-close, backdrop (matched by exact target so clicks inside the popup don't close it), rc-restore-item (restoreDeletedItem), rc-restore-slot (restoreDeletedSlot — a full-slots restore currently surfaces the refusal toast; the D2 step is batch 3). A document-level Esc handler closes it. New relAge helper renders "just now"/"Nm ago"/"Nh ago"/"yesterday"/"N days ago"/"N weeks ago" from a full ISO timestamp. The popup sub-text derives the 7 and 4 from MAX_SLOT_TRASH / MAX_ITEM_TRASH rather than hardcoding them.

CSS (workspace-regimen.css): .rc-trigger; the popup — .rc-backdrop (position:fixed, dimmed, backdrop-filter blur), .rc-pop (~700px, max-height with internal scroll, a sticky header), .rc-gal / .rc-gtile mini-tiles (the same colour-block-over-white-tray composition as the live save tiles), .rc-item rows, .rc-btn-restore / .rc-btn-ghost, .rc-empty, all reduced-motion-guarded (a fade + rise only under prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference).

Timestamp change (state/regimen.ts + core/schemas/regimen.ts): a new nowStamp() returns a full ISO timestamp, and deleteSlot / saveRgRemoved / restoreDeletedSlot now stamp deletedAt / removedAt with it instead of the date-only today(). detail:
Three fixes Luneth found while testing the scanner live, all signed off and pushed.

1) LIVE FEEDBACK. He corrected a misread nutrient name and nothing confirmed it worked - no check appeared. Turned out to be three problems: the OCR was mislabeling "Fat" as "Oat" (the auto-corrector snapped the word "fat" onto "oat", both in its dictionary one letter apart); the standard panel labels (Total Fat, Cholesterol, etc.) weren't in the recognized list, so even a correct fix wouldn't show a check; and nothing re-checked a row as you typed. All fixed - "Total Fat" now reads right, corrections resolve to a check, and every keystroke re-checks the row live.

2) PROGRESS BOUNCE. Scanning a sideways/upside-down label made the progress bar jump 0->100 several times - the offline orientation detector reads the image at up to 4 angles and each read restarted the bar. Now it fills once and the sweep runs under a smooth indeterminate animation.

3) HORIZONTAL PANELS. A small cheese tub (label-test-2) prints its whole nutrition panel as one long comma-separated line; the parser expected one nutrient per line and only got Protein + Fiber. Added comma-segment parsing. Honest ceiling: that tub's OCR also mangles the amounts and its minerals show only % DV (no absolute value), so it improved 2->4, not to perfection - the Confirm screen (now with live feedback) covers the rest. On a clean synthetic horizontal panel it recovers 10.

summary: WF-cheese ingredient read: scan grabbed the 'DISTRIBUTED BY' text, not the real ingredients, so no villains flagged. Fix: header line-anchored + headerless heuristic (comma-rich run after the last %DV). label-test-2 now flags modified/processed; no regression.
detail:
The cheese-tub scan (label-test-2) was reading the wrong text as its ingredient list - it pulled the "DISTRIBUTED BY / Whole Foods Market / www..." line instead of the actual ingredients, so none of the bad ingredients (like modified cornstarch) were flagged.

Root cause: the OCR garbles the real "INGREDIENTS:" header on this label, and the only clean word "INGREDIENTS" left in the text is the trailing allergen line "CONTAINS MILK INGREDIENTS." - the old regex matched THAT and captured everything after it, which was the distributor block.

Fix: the ingredients header must now sit at a line start (so it can no longer match the mid-sentence "MILK INGREDIENTS"), and for labels whose header is garbled the ingredient list is found structurally - it is the comma-rich run that comes AFTER the nutrition panel. Nutrition panels are full of "% DV" and ingredient lists have none, so we slice from the last "% DV" to the end, after cutting off the distributor / contact tail.

TECH -- state/ocr.ts parseOcrText:
- Header regex line-anchored: /(?:^|\n)[^\S\n]{0,8}(?:OTHER\s+)?INGREDIENTS?.../i (still allows supplement "Other Ingredients:"), plus a reject if the capture starts with distributor/manufactured/packed boilerplate.
- New headerless heuristic (only runs if nothing else set ingredients): body = whitespace-collapsed rawText, truncated at the first of DISTRIBUTED BY / MANUFACTURED BY / PACKED BY / www. / http(s) / (c); then start = end of the LAST "% DV" match (fallback: end of the last "Protein Ng"); take body.slice(start), strip leading punctuation, require >=3 commas and 30-2000 chars.

summary: Scanner hero reframed: 'covers N of 90' (full Wallach targets, ~always 0, a stack funnel) -> the ITEM's 'hits N of 90' (>=3% of Wallach's target). Pumpkin now 'Worth adding · delivers 6 · 2 strongly'. + fixed the Copper->'Pepper' parse bug. 00.A-clean.
detail:
Luneth scanned pumpkin seeds — one of the most nutritious foods there is — and the scanner said "0 reach the 90 this scan". He pushed back hard, and he was right: the scanner was headlining how many of the 90 essentials a scan got you to FULLY cover (a full Wallach daily target). Wallach's targets are so high that no real food, and no single supplement, hits even one of them alone — only the whole Youngevity stack (Ultimate Daily + EFA Plus + Tangy Tangerine + Ultimate Classic ...) approaches full coverage. So a "covers N of 90" headline is always ~0 and quietly turns the scanner into a funnel to buy the entire program, which is the opposite of its job: helping people judge which foods and supplements are worth introducing.

THE FIX, in two parts.

1. The scanner headline is now the ITEM's "hits N of 90" — how many essentials it delivers a MEANINGFUL amount of, defined as >= 3% of the Wallach daily target (his call, grounded on the real pumpkin numbers below). This scales honestly: a whole food hits ~6, a strong multivit far more, the full stack ~90 — so the number actually moves and discriminates. Crucially it is NOT called "covered": 3% is a meaningful start, not a full dose, and the wording says so. The full-target truth still lives on the Coverage tab (where YOU stand); the scanner answers "how good is this ITEM". Two honest jobs.

2. Copper bug: the OCR auto-corrector (ocrFuzzyFix) only skipped words it already knew as food terms, so a recognized nutrient-panel label like "Copper" — which is in the known-nutrients list but not the food-term list — got snapped to the nearest food word, "Pepper" (and "Phosphorus" -> "Phosphoric"), silently dropping them from the scan. Now it also skips anything in the known-nutrients list.

00.A: the 3% threshold is a DISPLAY threshold, always measured against the Wallach target.low (never an RDV/DV), and only the ~38 essentials Wallach has actually dosed are eligible. Where Wallach is silent there is no target to measure against, so the nutrient cannot be a hit (an honest non-hit — e.g. phosphorus, which pumpkin seeds have in quantity but Wallach never dosed).

REAL NUMBERS (his pumpkin label through the live engine, % of the Wallach target): Magnesium 20.8, Manganese 18.2, Copper 9.7, Iron 4.3, Zinc 4.3, Potassium 3.6, Selenium 1.6, Phosphorus 0 (no Wallach dose). At >= 3%: hits 6 (Fe, Mg, Zn, Cu, Mn, K) — exactly the set he intuited, including hard-to-get potassium. Strong (>= 10%): 2 (Mg, Mn). His literal "5%" intuition would have given only 2, because Wallach's targets run ~5-15x the RDV — a genuinely useful correction that came out of grounding the number in the real engine.

RESULT: pumpkin seeds now read "Aligns · Worth adding · Meaningfully delivers 6 of your 90 essentials · hit in a meaningful amount, a real start not a full daily target · 2 delivered strongly · 0 ingredient flags".

- state/scanner.ts — meaningfulHits() returns { hits, strong }; HIT_THRESHOLD 0.03, HIT_STRONG 0.10; ScanResult gains hits/hitEssentials/hitsStrong (interface only, recomputed per scan).
- views/scanner.ts — renderResult(): dropped delta/added/gaps; deck + gauge (single green hit-arc) + caption + facts all reframed to the item-hits story.
- workspace-scanner.css — .vd-cov-arc-cov/.vd-cov-arc-add -> .vd-cov-arc-hit.
- state/ocr.ts — ocrFuzzyFix skips known nutrient labels (dict.knownLower).

summary: Dark theme: brightened every non-orange/yellow foreground colour (text, links, labels, icons, borders) app-wide so it reads on charcoal; solid buttons stay vivid. Also fixed the profile popup — bigger tiny text, no bright grey pills, Cream/Charcoal previews, accent search icon.
detail:
The dark theme's non-orange/yellow colours were all too dark to read as foreground on charcoal. This sweep brightens them everywhere they're used as text, links, labels, icons, or borders, while keeping the solid coloured buttons/pills vivid. Plus a full pass on the profile popup. Luneth signed off the tint level + full-sweep scope mid-way.

WHY IT WAS HARD: every colour token is dual-use — the same token colours foreground text AND fills a hover/count pill that carries white text on it. So a token can't be blanket-brightened without turning a button white-on-light. A 3-agent map found ~370 foreground uses across ~12 token families.

THE FIX (token-level where safe, targeted where not):
1. --ds-accent-deep is a FOREGROUND-only accent role → remapped in dark to color-mix(--ds-accent 55%, --ds-ink), a bright light tint of the live accent. One line fixes ~70 accent eyebrows/labels/links/dose-values and the active nav tab.
2. Facet + entity tokens (--fam-science/action/story; search --t-element/condition/concept/substance/topic) brightened at the token level for the knowledge + search mounts → the EXPLORE topic pills + every facet number/dot/label read. The ~14 white-on-facet hover/count pills were re-pinned to their saturated hue (or flipped to dark text) so they still read on the now-light fill.
3. Bare --ds-accent used as foreground (text/border/thin-fill/svg — ~110 selectors from the agent map, shell + workspaces + drawers) routed to --ds-accent-deep. Accent FILLS stay saturated (a light primary button reads washed even if technically legible).
4. Status/tech foregrounds (--ds-status-ok/err/info, --ds-tech, --ds-tech-dim, --ds-ok-deep) → color-mix(token 62%, --ds-ink) in the matching property.
5. Hardcoded dark hexes: the mineral deep-dive's theme-unaware `--ds-accent:#2b6fb0` override, vitamin-A pro/con lead text (#2f7a33/#b0442e), and the seven-entry product delivery-form palette.
6. Profile popup: .pf-eyebrow/.pf-namemeta/.pf-label/.pf-log__sum 0.56–0.58rem → 0.65rem; .pf-fchip background:transparent (the "bright inactive pills" were the browser's default #f0f0f0 button face showing through — no background was set); .pf-modeb rebuilt as theme previews (Cream = light bg + dark text, Charcoal = dark bg + light text, active = accent ring); .kd-search-icon --ds-tech → --ds-accent-deep so it follows the chosen accent; avatar monogram pinned light so it reads on the saturated accent disc.

EXCLUDED: ORAC internals (that surface is being redesigned); the coverage/regimen goal-and-category runtime colours (--gc/--tc/--cc/--sc, user-chosen, out of scope); primary-button label colour on the darkest accents (a fill, pre-existing, left for a possible follow-up).

The in-app browser pane would not display, so everything was rendered headless via Puppeteer with a seeded dark profile and read with getComputedStyle. Not pushed.

METHOD NOTE for next time: getComputedStyle returns brightened color-mix values as `color(srgb 0..1)` floats, NOT rgb(0..255) — a contrast checker that assumes 0–255 will report light-on-dark as ~1:1 (all false positives). Parse the color() float form and composite alpha before judging.

summary: Fixed three dark-theme controls Luneth spotted: the profile Done button (washed-out on every accent), the recycle Restore hover (its own text unreadable), and the scanner delete-row X hover (glowed the accent instead of red).
detail:
Three small dark-theme fixes, all reported by Luneth in one session. In the dark theme, three buttons were still wearing colours chosen for the light theme: (1) the profile "Done" button looked pale and desaturated for every accent colour; (2) the recycle-bin "Restore" button turned so pale when hovered that its own light text became unreadable; (3) the little "X" that deletes a row in the label scanner lit up in the chosen accent colour on hover, when a delete control should always read RED.

All three trace to a single root cause. The dark-theme sweep deliberately remaps one accent token, --ds-accent-deep, to a pale light tint so it reads as bright TEXT on charcoal. But these three spots were using that same token as a solid FILL, so the fill washed out. The delete button had a second problem: it is a .ui-close, so the app-wide "close buttons hover in the accent colour" rule was overriding its own red hover rule.

Fix — one new block in theme.css (the non-sealed appearance layer), all :root[data-theme="dark"]-scoped:
(J6) FILL restores → route to the SATURATED per-accent var(--ds-accent-hot), which the sweep left untouched:
  - .pf-done gradient deep end: var(--ds-accent-deep) → var(--ds-accent-hot)
  - .rc-btn-restore:hover background: var(--ds-accent-deep) → var(--ds-accent-hot)
(J7) destructive-hue carve-out:
  - .vd-nrow__del.ui-close:hover border-color → color-mix(in srgb, var(--ds-status-err) 55%, var(--ds-ink))
  - the two-class selector (specificity 0,5,0) outranks the generic :is(..., .ui-close:hover, ...) accent-border rule (0,4,0), so RED wins on every accent, independent of source order
  - the err is brightened to mirror accent-deep's own formula, so the rim stays exactly as visible as the accent rim it replaces — only red
  - cream already hovered red (the accent-close rule is dark-only), so this restores light/dark parity

No sealed pillar touched; no JS changed; eden/ untouched.

  - invariants 92/92 (incl. css_comment_no_premature_close and workspace_coverage_no_dead_rules green; 111 class selectors all live)
